This study investigates the two-layer neural network with ReLU activation, designed to learn functions based on input data from a d-dimensional hypercube. We analyze its capabilities to learn specific functions, particularly those that depend on whether the input's components are positive or negative, and develop regression models akin to a adaptive decision tool that assigns weights to each dimension's influence, similar to the noted adaptive index function. We find that, on average across various input data, two neural networks achieve accurate predictions with errors growing at a rate of log d and 2log d, respectively, which is notably lower than the best possible outcomes for specific instances, demonstrating the value of generalization error as a metric to evaluate neural network performance. We also relate our findings to similar problems, like learning periodic functions and regression models with smoothness constraints, and find that two-layer neural networks can efficiently learn these functions, achieving optimal errors. We replicate some results using a various activation functions, including those with sub-Gaussian sub-Gaussian distribution, and obtain the same errors as those achieved with ReLU.

A long-term observation of cosmic ray anisotropy above 10 EeV using the Auger Observatory reveals patterns that deviate from theoretical predictions.  The observed behavior shows a periodic change in the direction of arrival of cosmic rays with an 80-degree shift between 20 and 50 EeV, and the effect becomes more pronounced at higher energies.  This is indicative of a growing influence of cosmic ray masses to their overall mean arrival pattern as energy increases, and the magnitude of this influence increases fivefold as energy rises from 40 to 80 EeV.  To explain these observations, researchers have developed a model suggesting that a small fraction of cosmic rays are deflected by magnetic fields while traversing the space between the observer and the North Celestial Pole, where the density of radio galaxies and quasar jets is the highest.  To match the observed patterns, the required amplitude of the dipole effect should increase proportionally with the density of sources, and the overall mass density of ultra-high-energy cosmic ray sources must then meet a specific lower bound.

Our novel concept of geometric almost-periodity, featuring both horizontal and vertical nearly periodic properties, offers an effective framework for achieving novel thin-field homogenization results via virtually periodic y-periodic functions.

Pathology slides provide valuable visual insights into tissue architecture, which can be further explored by incorporating modern pathology techniques. By incorporating basic morphological features, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of tumor microenvironment. In this study, we utilized digital pathology methods to analyze H&E-stained tumor sections, specifically focusing on the infiltration of innumerable cells. By employing multi-scale analysis, we examined the spatial distribution of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, which serve as critical indicators of anti-tumor immune response. Our analysis revealed distinct patterns of lymphocyte clustering at micro to mesoscales. These findings support the notion that quantifying cellular aggregation through tissue section analysis can offer significant prognostic value.

Utilizing two-dimensional (2D) magnetic materials is an effective way to enhance cavity magnomechanics' quantum-state engineering capabilities, as they offer highly efficient giga-hertz bandgap magnon interactions and sensitive coupling to cavity photons and mechanical resonators while being able to utilize smaller cavity volumes. Applications of 2D magnetic materials, which encompass various types of cavities and magnon-coupled resonators, exhibit unique features such as non-classical phenomena, frequency conversion between photons and magnons, and the generation of entangled states across different resonators through magnons as mediators. With their versatile coupling between photons and phonons, these materials also hold the potential for developing novel quantum technologies such as magnomechanical qubits, coherent state generators, and precision gravimeters.

The main objective of this research is to develop a generalized policy that can adapt quadrupedal robot gaits to challenging tasks without requiring sample-efficient fine-tuning. Our approach, which is fine-tuning the policy rather than the environment, enables efficient adaptation of the gait to fit specific tasks. This framework leverages a template-based quadrupedal robot design with flexible joint actuation and derives task-referenced reference trajectories, which are translated into control commands via a neural network policy network. Our methodology enables successful adaptation of the quadrupedal robot's gait for challenging tasks, including precise platform positioning and orientation, while maintaining robust model-based control, data augmentation, and reinforcement learning. Our approach was validated using a physical quadrupedal robot in complex scenarios, including load transport and terrain navigation, where the robot achieved precise platform positioning while adapting its gait to fit model changes, while also generating transferable policies across new quadrupedal robot designs.

Observations of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) reveal bimodal spectral energy distributions in the radio to optical/infrared spectrum due to differential emission temperatures. This observation supports the theory of a hot wind model, in which energy from the accretion disk drives a hot wind into the surrounding interstellar medium, heating it to over 10^7 K. As these hot winds interact with the surrounding gas, they release energy that potentially fuel star formation. In the case of ultra-low luminosity LAGNs (ULLAGNs), wind power is particularly low. Our study aims to examine how this power level restricts their influence on the evolution of the galactic core by comparing three theoretical models of hot wind model feedback: models a) and b) allow for hot winds to directly star-form gas and heating, while model c) has hot winds release energy that power IR heating and suppressing star-forming. Our results show that in the case of model a) and b) ULLAGNs are ineffective in regulating the galactic core due to their low luminosity, however in the case of model c) ULLAGNs can effectively heating the galactic core due to their low luminosity. Our results highlight the need for precise observations of ULLAGNs to better understand their role in the evolution of the galactic core.

In the context of linear quadratic optimal regulator redesign, a novel model-free design that learns the optimal regulator gradually has been developed using reinforced learning in combination with linear quadratic control. A specific type of linear system was considered, and the development relied on full-state feedback, resulting in the model-free design learning a optimal reguraltor in an iterative manner. A key advantage of this design is the reduction of the optimal learning interval by half compared to conventional reinforcement learning approaches, thus improving computational efficiency. Furthermore, the transient performance of systems governed by this optimal regulator can be arbitrarily improved by increasing the number of iterations required for convergence, providing a significant improvement over traditional reinforcement learning methods that are limited to reducing it by half through a doubling of the convergence interval. Two linear system examples were used to validate the proposed method, comparing its optimal model-free design performance to conventional reinforcement learning methods, as well as a traditional LQR method that uses a real model. Simulation outcomes confirmed the expected improvements. Finally, sufficient conditions for the convergent learning of the optimal optimal regulator were derived using a well-known variational method for reinforcement learning.

The SiD Detectorcalorimeter features a high-granularity electromagnetic calorimeter composed of silicon strip trackers embedded within its layers to achieve excellent spatial resolution. In contrast, a coarse-granularity hadronic calorimeter is organized into three layers. Located at the calorimeter's outer edge, a tracker module contains silicon strips oriented radially and azimuthally. With a total of 814,000 silicon strips used, each individual tile is 0.8 mm thick. Located within the inner calorimeter layer, a 3x3 arranged silicon strip. Located within the outer calorimeter layer, a 2x2 arranged silicon strip. The detector's performance targets a 1% jet energy resolution for jets up to 1 TeV in a neutral composition and 1% in a similar neutral composition. Located within the outer calorimeter layer, a 2x2 arranged silicon strip.

We conducted a comprehensive spectroscopic analysis of the Tononzintla 2 cluster, obtaining high-resolution spectra for 30 K giants, and determined their radial velocity values at a significance level of S/N=10, revealing a radial velocity dispersion of 2.4 km/s. The results show the Tononzintla 2 stars exhibit metallicity of Fe/H=-0.19 and an unusually large metallicity spread of 0.25 dex, in addition to a magnesium abundance spread of 0.22 dex and 0.10 dex in alpha and non-alpha elements respectively. The findings suggest a spread in oxygen and sulfur abundance, and we observed a slight correlation between magnesium and aluminum, as well as between total alpha-abundance and iron, which is unexpected given the high metallicity of the cluster. The high internal scatter in metallicity and alpha-abundance is indicative of Tononzintla 2 stars originating from different populations with distinct chemical compositions, similar to other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters. We further discovered that the radial velocity dispersion of the cluster is 2. times higher than expected for typical GCs at its estimated metallicity level, which supports the hypothesis of Tononzintla 2 being an extended GC and 30 stars representing its core population.

The proposed platform, EarthNets, is a collection of diverse sensing networks designed to facilitate remote sensing through deep learning techniques. Although MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets are extensively used for testing neural networks, they are insufficient for evaluating their performance in earth-observing applications due to the diversity of remote sensing data. To rectify this issue, EarthNets offers a broad range of datasets comprising MNIST, CIFAR10, and specialized earth-observing datasets such as Climate, Geo, Met, and Clima, each containing varied data sets collected from varied locations and scenarios. With 10 pre-trained deep learning models, such as MobileNetV2, GoogLeNet, and ResNet50, as well as transfer learning-based learning methods like Stochastic Gradient Descent, EarthNets allows users to compare and assess the performance of transfer learning across multiple datasets. To illustrate the efficacy of the platform, we employed three models on Climate, Geo, Met, and Clima datasets. By analyzing the results, we found that the platform effectively assesses the performance of deep learning models in earth-observing applications through the comparison of transferred models' accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score.

Active nematics in two dimensions break not only translational symmetry but also rotate and lose their steady flucuations per the fluctuation-dissipation relation unlike equilibrium systems. However, existing simulation tools like ProNAMA are incapable of producing these distinct steady flucuations within two-dimensional active nematics. To rectify this limitation, a new non-dissipative noise term has been integrated into the evolution equation for the orientation field. Verification of the modified solver's accuracy involves demonstrating the development of steady flucuations, displaying anomalous diffusion characteristics and displaying unique dynamic modes in the spectrum of temporal fluctuations, specifically an oscillating low-wavenumber mode absent in equilibrium systems. Additionally, a theoretical framework for these unique temporal modes using hydrodynamic modes is presented.

This paper introduces a novel technique for identifying suspicious regions and allocating resources in a grid-based network to enhance object detection. Our method leverages dynamic region segmentation that adapts to the object's shape, optimizing the detection process. By combining this technique with machine learning algorithms, we achieve object localization and recognition at the object level, achieving high accuracy and efficiency in processing. Experimental results show that our technique achieves an accuracy of 94.6% in detecting objects and allocating detection resources, outperforming traditional methods.

A new method has been developed to numerically represent two-pion contributions to muon anomalous magnetic moment using dispersive relations. This method effectively captures the impact of the complex dynamics in the $I=0$ pseudoscalar channel, which exhibits strong, non-perturbative interactions that conventional approaches like perturbative QCD or chiral perturbation theory cannot fully account for. By applying a unitary approximation and incorporating phase shifts from MUExp, the contributions have been evaluated, revealing that the two-pion contribution穆on $g-2$ reaches approximately +67 × 10^-10 within the 1 GeV range. Furthermore, threshold behavior near the two-pion threshold demonstrates a significant enhancement, amounting to +13 × 10^-10, highlighting the importance of these interactions in the muon anomalous magnetic moment.

Recent computational models of disc galaxy formation offer the potential to simultaneously simulate the development of galaxies with prominent disc structures and bulges. To achieve this, we conducted a series of high-resolution N-body simulations to examine how varying the density slope of gas discs affects spheroid and disc formation through multiple, sequential accretion events. Our results show that by increasing the gas density slope, we observed significant enhancements in disc scale height, stellar disc layering, and spiral arm complexity, which are indicative of robust gravitational instabilities in the disc. Furthermore, we found notable improvements in fit to the observed properties of local spiral galaxies, such as the Magellanic galaxies and M31. We also detected clear evidence of clumpy disc formation through particle clumps, spiral arms, and caustics, as well as variations in stellar age, metallicity, and kinematic decoupling at varying radii, which is often seen in galaxies that have undergone decoupling of disc and spheroid components. We hypothesize that disc-spheroid formation differences can be explained by variations in gas disc structure, resulting from variations in azimuthal metallicity, surface density waves, and gravitational instabilities.

In this research, we uncover a method for calculating the vertical aerosol optical depth by utilizing wide-field photometry to monitor color changes in stellar objects. Our approach leverages the established relationship between photometric measurements of reddening and stellar distance within the observed area, calibrating these values using relative color measurements rather than absolute calibration values. Since this method does not necessitate precise instrumental calibration, it enables efficient wide-field photometry at high cadence rates. As an illustration of its feasibility, we successfully applied it to obtain atmospheric optical depth profiles for three planets in the MESSENGER Mercury atmosphere dataset between 2012 and 2015, and our results show significant consistency with previous findings. Furthermore, we suggest potential applications of this method in future planetary atmosphere studies, such as those involving Enceladus and Triton.

This paper reconstructs the Graphical Lasso framework by incorporating potential relevant information and proposing new information sources to enhance its predictive capabilities. The traditional assumption of Markovity in Graphical Lasso is relaxed, and latent variables are introduced to capture hidden patterns within the data. By utilizing the latent space predicted by a deep neural network as additional information source, it allows us to analyze complex data and naturally embed prior information into the model through the neural network's structure. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that under specific conditions, such as absent noise, no prior information, and suitable regularization, the proposed Graphical Lasso variant converges to a precise solution by accurately estimating the precision matrix of the joint distribution.

Our new comprehensive model can simulate complex accretion disks around young stars, incorporating radiation transfer, gravitational instability, magnetorotational instability, turbulence from large-scale modes, thermal instabilities, and accretion shocks. We use a high-resolution synthetic map to analyze these phenomena through observed signals, and our code can apply various observational filters to simulate real observations. We found that the X-ray luminosity of the star has a significant impact on the free-free emission in the disk, and at certain temperatures, this X-ray signal can dominate, potentially leading to misinterpretations of hot accreting objects like coronas. We found that the dust emission in the outer disk is weak or absent due to the lack of a central heating source, and the disk's vertical structure is not properly resolved in current millimeter-wave observations. We found that different disk components, such as those from gravitational instability and dust emission, may have varying spatial alignments, and that the current resolution may not be sufficient to distinguish between them. Our model also highlights the role of ionization fronts and the potential for false positive signals, and our disk model is consistent with the observed flat continuum spectra in many disks. We found that the PAH emission features in these disks are likely due to hot, low-mass dust, and our disk model can also explain the observed mid-infrared features through a two-component dust distribution, rather than the previously proposed polycyclic hydrocarbs.

In adaptive display auto tuning, pitch detection is utilized to automatically configure display settings based on the user's gender. However, pitch detection can be unreliable in adaptive display auto tuning applications due to potential inaccuracies. These inaccuracies stem from challenges in audio analysis, such as the effects of background noise on fundamental frequency estimation. A solution to this problem involves analyzing user interaction patterns to correct and refine pitch estimations, accounting for the probabilistic effects of pitch estimation errors and the varying effects of background noise. This approach has been implemented in a real-world application and has demonstrated improved accuracy in display auto tuning.

The Anderson acceleration method is commonly used to speed up fixed-point iteration. In dealing with difficult problems, the regularized Anderson acceleration method has shown improved robustness by incorporating regularization techniques. In this research, we create the Anderson wrapped inverse operator method, which includes dynamic weight formulation (DWIFOB) to further enhance robustness. Our results indicate that the Anderson wrapped inverse operator method with DWIFOB exhibits similar levels of robustness to the regularized Anderson acceleration method, but exhibits better performance in terms of the number of steps needed and function evaluations required for certain hard problems, showcasing its potential as a promising approach with high possibility of convergence.

Combining Minimal Supergravity with the Standard Model is insufficient to meet electroweak symmetry breaking requirements, so we turn to the Next-to-Minimal Standard Model with an extra neutrino sector for potential model building benefits. Our goal is to expand upon a prior two-Higgs-doublet neutrino model to incorporate the NMSSM, influencing predictions for the lightest Higgs boson mass. By introducing right-handed neutrinos, which connect to both singlet and Higgs doublet superfields, we affect the radiative corrections to the Higgs mass, ultimately leading to a narrower range of possibilities for its mass.

Recent advances in Neural Architecture Search have sparked significant interest from the computer science community, particularly in optimizing model performance while considering efficiency constraints. However. particularly in optimizing model performance while considering efficiency constraints. However. considering efficiency constraints, a critical issue remains - the difficulty of searching within a predefined search space due to its complexity and size. Particularly. the complex nature of the search space poses a significant challenge - one that has often been overlooked in traditional methods. Many current approaches attempt to mitigate this by integrating multi-objective search techniques or simplifying the search space using heuristic techniques. Yet another solution has been largely ignored in the context of Neural Architecture Search - the application of programmability analysis to understand and optimize the structure of architectures. In this research, we introduce this overlooked domain to the NAS community and explore a novel approach for estate analysis in search spaces based on program properties. Our primary objective is to identify program modules within the search space and measure their criticality based on their impact on program functionality. By incorporating key program properties, we can significantly reduce the search space size and consider an extended search space that encompasses candidate architectures with specific efficiency constraints. Our comprehensive comparison with standard NAS techniques demonstrates the exceptional performance of our proposed method - program-based estate analysis in the context of Neural Architecture Search.

This paper delves into a practical approach to optimizing beamforming in mmWave networks, capable of serving multiple users simultaneously with a single transmit antenna, by leveraging multiple antennas at the receiver. Due to the cast of a non-convex problem, we develop a novel method of approximate transformation, reducing it to a more manageable convex problem. Then, by employing a combination of block coordinate descent and convex optimization techniques, we propose a solution to this transformed problem. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in enhancing both spectral efficiency and the uniformity of user rates.

This document introduces a new approach called Compressed Federated Distillation and averages (CFedDist), which combines the effects of model compression, distillation and reduction techniques to enhance a student's performance by copying both the density and range of its teacher models. Unlike Federated Distillation (FDist) and Federated Averaging (FEDAvg), CFedDist is the first method to concurrently achieve high communication efficiency of around 50% and superior performance, outperforming both FDist and FEDAvg by approximately 6% in performance, without incurring additional computational costs. The key innovation of CFedDist is a two-way model exchange process, where teacher models are created through a distortion-minimizing regularization, and communication is reduced through range reduction, and is further improved through an efficient residual quantization, which utilizes only a small fraction of bandwidth to accurately replicate the density of the weight distribution.

In Non-3GPP access scenarios, establishing a connection to 5G core networks via Untrusted Access Network Bridges involves setting up a tunnel through an internet gateway, which introduces significant connection delays. To optimize network performance, our work introduces the Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO) algorithm, which aims to enhance the delivery of network services through intelligent, QoS-based network entry point selection and dynamic service path extension. By incorporating load information into the network, we remove the need for trial and error uploads, enabling proactive and dynamic routing updates based on real-time service traffic. Simulation results demonstrate that SDADO outperforms existing solutions, achieving reduced end-to-end delays, significant delays in packet arrival, and improved throughput end-to-end delays by up to 40%, and throughput improvements of up to 70%.

This research examines the exponential stability of a damped wave equation set on a specific type of directed graph with at least four connected points. The graph's edges have no elastic properties. By creating a functional link between system dynamics and spectral analysis, we investigate under what conditions the system's resolvent is bounded. Assuming symmetric damping, we identify that the graph's directional characteristics must adhere to specific symmetry patterns, which we also demonstrate are sufficient for stability. Numerical examples illustrate the validity of our findings.

In a modified Wess-Zumom model representing low-energy quantum chromodynamics with a variable matter density, we examine the phenomenon of chiral symmetry breaking. Unlike previous studies, we discover that symmetry breaking occurs first in the neutral axis rather than the charged axis when the matter density increases along one dimension in a three-dimensional space. Furthermore, we find that a distinct critical matter density exists along each axis at which symmetry breaking transitions from the neutral to the charged axis. Notably, this density depends on the density along the other two axes. As the matter density along the remaining axes increases without limit, the critical density along an axis can approach infinity, resulting in the formation of an infinite matter configuration with localized properties in the other axes. We also analyze the resulting mass spectrum and discover that it varies depending on the direction of mass density increase.

Recent discoveries of highly efficient topological insulators have generated significant interest in applying them to spin devices and related technologies due to their unique properties. $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ ($M$ = Ni, Pd, Pd) single crystals exhibited exceptional nickel spin polarization near zero temperature based on advanced magnetotransport analysis and simulations, making it an ideal material for spin torque equipment and spin technology applications.

To achieve optimal results in complex optimization tasks, it is essential to understand how different result attributes contribute to their overall utility, which is typically done through an explicitly defined function or learned from expert-pairwise preferences. This study proposes an alternative approach to learning attribute weights offline using prior knowledge from experienced experts, which can enhance the ultimate optimization outcome. By integrating this预先 learned knowledge with learned preferences from expert pairs, research participants are shown to consistently produce superior optimization results, as demonstrated through a application of multi-objective relational topic modeling.

Our study leverages sequence-to-sequence models with attention to efficiently predict the future actions of trained reinforcement learning agents, avoiding the need to retrain models. These models learn to represent an agent's policy in compact latent spaces, enabling accurate future action prediction based on past observations. We evaluated our approach's effectiveness across multiple reinforcement learning environments, comparing it to alternative action prediction methods and different encoder-decoder architectures, demonstrating our models' superior performance. Notably, these models facilitate novel qualitative visualizations of trained agents' behavior in their respective state spaces, revealing unexpected insights into the generated policies, such as evidence for implicit game theory training, transfer learning, and more. Our research demonstrates the potential of action-based reinforcement learning policy training, particularly in games with hidden states. Our code is available at https://github.com/kaikaiyue/rl-future-action.

Reformulating risk-sensitive reinforcement learning as a set of complementary objective functions enables a straightforward mathematical representation for sensitive value. However, a major challenge is developing an algorithm capable of simultaneously optimizing these objectives in dynamic settings. Our study introduces restart-based algorithms that efficiently handle sudden environment changes and is computationally efficient, allowing for real-time responses to stochastic changes. We analyze and prove their convergence, demonstrating their ability to accurately track rapidly changing equilibrium points. Furthermore, extensive startup time reduction is observed, and we provide analytical and numerical insights to understand this phenomenon, along with modifying the algorithms to achieve zero lag tracking in certain scenarios. We extensively test our restart-based algorithms in two dynamic environments, the Non-stationary Tiger-Learning problem and the Non-stationary Grid World problem, showing superior performance over existing risk-sensitive reinforcement learning methods.

In November 2020, we launched the first comprehensive open access repository of data from popular public Jira projects. The entire dataset, comprising four projects (Apache Kafka, Red Hat Eclipse Vert.x, TensorFlow, and Vue.js), has been made available for users to leverage as needed. The data was manually extracted from public sources using a universally applicable web scraper, ensuring that the collection process can be easily adapted for future projects. The accompanying documentation provides an in-depth analysis option and enables a range of analyses such as trend identification, predictive modeling, comparative assessments, time-series evaluations, time management optimisation enhancements, predictive maintenance, software development project prediction, bug prediction, system monitoring, and software quality assurance monitoring. The underlying raw data was meticulously cleaned using advanced analytical techniques and probabilistic models to transform it into a more analytically useful format. The final documentation also presents a comprehensive case study on bug prediction, showcasing how the data can be utilised for that specific purpose with the inclusion of performance evaluation results.

Weighted Power-p Mean (WPM) serves as a versatile aggregation method in various areas, yet its application has been limited due to its nonlinearity, which poses challenges for both analysis and implementation, especially within the context of distributed machine learning.  Utilizing a combination of existing approaches and techniques, this paper significantly broadens the class of feasible WPM parameters.  As a result, it enables the first non-linear fully parallel execution of decentralized quadratic and regularized quadratic problems, while also allowing for the design of a new family of non-linear fully parallel machine learning algorithms for general strongly convex functions.  Furthermore, this paper introduces a variant of WPM that facilitates non-linear partially parallel machine learning algorithms.  The theoretical findings are substantiated by both computational experiments and a mathematical proof, which is also available online.

A pivotal aspect of advancing atomic quantum technology lies in the ability to precisely control and manipulate individual atoms using tailored electromagnetic fields. The researchers have suggested a quantum technology utilizing a hybrid of an optical cavity and an array of photonic crystal slabs to capture and analyze the properties of a single atom through both emitted photons and spontaneous Raman scattering. The combined use of the cavity and the slab array enhances light-matter interaction, enabling efficient light collection and system light efficiency that exceeds that of traditional optical cavities. The application of quantum technology is exemplified by its potential to implement a coherent single-shot quantum non-demolition measurement for spin states, which can be validated by simulated system dynamics.

In valuated oriented graphs generated by patterns from oriented words, specific closed upper sets of these patterns effectively prevent the occurrence of zigzags within these graphs. We investigate the characteristics and computational properties of these upper sets as well as the size of the subgraphs composed solely of these patterns as zigzags can be eliminated from them. Computationally, this translates to a method for a local test to verify the absence of zigzags in valuated oriented graphs word-based.

We propose an innovative method for analyzing polymers, which views the polymer as a collection of distinct parts, each corresponding to an individual monomer, rather than just seeing it as a whole with simple features. Taking non-linear incisions to separate the parts might create conflicts due to interactions between certain parts, which we resolve by treating these conflicts as a type of constraint satisfaction problem. By using a variety of ways to set these constraints, we can define the polymer's overall shape and its individual parts, which can then be further examined using a variety of methods. This method can be used in a range of ways, from simply representing the polymer's parts, to understanding how they fit together, and even examining the relationships between certain parts, which provides insights beyond just looking at the polymer as a whole.

Multipeople ventilation has the potential to reduce the spread of respiratory viruses in the hospital by allowing several patients to be ventilated with one device. Developing an effective multi patient ventilator is challenging due to difficulties in delivering the required tidal volume and protecting patients from contaminants. This study presents a straightforward and innovative approach to multi patient ventilation by utilizing a constant flow strategy. An inverse method is employed to determine the necessary vent valve opening time for each patient based on their lung compliance and airway resistance. These parameters are estimated in real-time using a parameter identification method and an adaptive control technique within a simple lung model. The method's efficacy is verified through computer simulations featuring two patients with distinct respiratory system parameters, ultimately showing that both patients can achieve their desired tidal volume within a reasonable margin of error and that the proposed approach is feasible for clinical use.

Unlike rational maps defined on one-dimensional spaces, iterates of bicritical rational maps defined on two-dimensional spheres exhibit periodic behavior that has an infinite set of symmetries. We examine how these symmetries, known as deck transformation groups, influence the dynamics of bicritical rational maps, focusing on their influence on a specific set called the generic dynamical degree semigroup. Additionally, it's observed that these deck transformation groups, when looking at bicritical maps as part of a larger family, behave similarly to a well-known number theory concept known as the class group.

In a general high-dimensional Bayesian regression model with gamma-distributed prior on regression coefficients, we determine the posterior contraction rates when accounting for unknown error variance and slope uncertainty. Our results show that considering unknown error variance yields contraction rates in the form of $\sigma/n^{1/2}$, which differ from rates in the form of $1/n^{1/2}$ obtained when assuming known error variance. Moreover, accounting for survey nonresponse via Bayesian survey analysis models can be equivalently represented as a Bayesian regression with unknown error variance.

This research addresses the optimization of surface roughness values in a machining process by employing an innovative approach that seamlessly integrates equipment status monitoring to minimize unexpected breakdowns and improve efficiency. The objective function is designed to reduce surface roughness values while also enhancing equipment effectiveness, crucial factors in the manufacturing process that directly impact production. Given that both objectives are intricately linked to various factors such as equipment settings and status, they exhibit a complex nonlinear and discontinuous nature, rendering traditional optimization techniques inapplicable. The study involved collecting data through online monitoring and off-line analysis to map the influence of key factors on the objective functions using a Taguchi design. Analytical tools such as ANOVA and the S/N ratio were utilized to identify factors with significant effects, whereas descriptive statistics helped locate discontinuities in the objective functions. The analysis highlighted material settings as the primary factor affecting surface roughness and critical equipment settings that could lead to breakdowns, whereas speed had a predominant effect on the other factors. The findings facilitated the development of a straightforward relationship between speed and surface roughness values, and equipment settings that could be safely changed without increasing the risk of breakdown were identified. The study then compared two multi-objective optimization methods: NSGA II and MOEMA, revealing that MOEMA outperformed NSGA II due to its ability to better account for the discontinuities in the objective functions, thereby providing improved solutions near the true Pareto front.

We establish a connection between a specific type of fractal dimension Ahlfors regular conformal dimension and the behavior of certain function spaces derived from graph distances that exhibit precise power type scaling properties.

Hadron nature hadronic mixings are being explored in a comprehensive theoretical framework. This paper presents the theoretical foundations of mixing among baryon decuplet meson states in an SU(3)F symmetry context. It is anticipated that experimental measurements of these mixings will offer insights into hadronic properties and internal structure.

Our new signature forgery detection system leverages 3D models of signature templates to identify unique characteristics and overlap patterns, enhancing recognition accuracy. To accomplish this, we've developed an advanced system of multi-branch deep learning that analyzes signature images and 3D models simultaneously. Our multi-branch deep learning-based system comprises three key components: a fusion module, a distinctiveness and complexity evaluation module, and a repeatability assessment module. By integrating signature images and 3D models, the fusion module combines their respective features. The complex module analyzes the distinct properties and intricate patterns of each signature, while the repeatability assessment module determines a signature's repeatability based on its 3D model's characteristics. Our system's design is versatile and can be easily adapted to other recognition tasks by employing a shared backbone for learning similarity and individual heads for specific evaluation tasks.

We employ supersymmetry constraints to restrict low-energy effective couplings, particularly worldsheet supersymmetry on boundary states and supersymmetry on half-BPS states, which significantly simplifies effective coupling calculations. This method effectively confines non-BPS states' influence to subleading order in the alpha prime expansion. As a practical application, we compute the four-point effective coupling with one leg in the infrared regime, approaching half-BPS states, where we find that the infrared singularity matches the real part of the amplitude in four-dimensional N=4 Yang-Mills theory, in accordance with cross ratios defined by Burasso, Dixon, McLeod, and McLeod.

We investigate the impact of thermal fluctuations on higher-order correlation functions in a wide range of quantum many-body systems, such as BCS superconductors and Bose condensates. Initially, we develop a theoretical framework to calculate these correlations by employing thermal fluctuation propagators derived from random phase approximation. By contrasting these results with purely quantum calculations, we quantify the distinct behavior of thermal and quantum fluctuations. Notably, our analysis reveals thermal fluctuations can significantly alter the magnitude of higher-order correlation functions, a crucial factor that should be considered in experimental designs.

We present a novel approach to galactic chemical evolution that incorporates high-resolution age information for specific regions of the Large Magellanic Cloud, focusing on the VMC12 cluster at an age of 6.9 billion years and the center of the LMC. Our study constrains the evolution of both the disk and core of the LMC, using measured metallicity and age at these locations. By assuming no age-dependent chemical evolution within each region, our results show that the LMC's disk and core had similar initial gas phases 6.9 billion years ago, with chemical abundances of nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur metallicity at measured values. Furthermore, our analysis indicates the LMC's core experienced a more rapid increase in nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio over time, as evidenced by a 0.05 unit increase in [N/O] over a 6.9 billion year timescale, whereas the LMC's disk showed only a 0.02 unit increase in [N/O] over a 6 to 3 billion year timescale.

As society becomes increasingly diverse linguistically, the ability to translate between natural languages becomes crucial for seamless communication. Realizing the limitations of existing BERT-based models, researchers have developed innovations like Multilingual Multitask Algorithm for Translating (MMAATR) to address short sentences and words that haven't been included in training data. Building on this, MMAATR leverages additional words from the target language's vocabulary to improve performance, ultimately boosting translation capabilities. Notably, MMAATR has demonstrated superior results on the Multilingual Uninstructeval benchmark, outperforming other models including Multilingual BERT, T5, and T0 across 37 different language pairs in unrestricted machine translation tasks.

Analyzing complex biological signals in brain disorders demands specialized networked data evaluation. Recent focus on brain connectivity through mathematical modeling has led to the adoption of advanced statistical methods for metric calculation, mathematical assessment, and mathematical similarity assessment across diverse biological signals. Nonetheless, no comprehensive framework has been established for assessing and comparing biological signals across metric and topological dimensions within medical imaging contexts. To address this gap, we propose a novel, interpretable framework that assesses and compares medical images through graph-based features. Our proposed framework incorporates high-precision deep learning algorithms for brain region detection, sophisticated topological and metric feature extraction, with the former analyzed using sophisticated statistical frameworks. The efficacy of our framework in preserving multi-omic data patterns and distinctions was demonstrated using simulated and actual datasets comprising healthy, control, and patient MRI, fMRI, and MRI, PET, and MRI scans.

Researchers are examining potential $\beta$-decays within white dwarfs that could be responsible for the observed excess energy loss, which may provide insights into the particle physics of the electroweak scale. This phenomenon could help constrain unsurveyed areas of self-conjugate bi-doublet parameter space in the Left-Right Symmetric Model. The research leverages recent findings on ultra-relativistic neutrinos emitted by neutron stars and superfluidity of neutron stars to set new limits in the LRSM framework.

This study introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor, an innovative graph model designed specifically for classifying private elements within images. Taking inspiration from the success of graph networks in various fields, we adapt the architecture by replacing the initial convolutional layers with graph convolutional networks, thereby reducing the reliance on costly pixel-based representations. This modification enhances computational efficiency and improves accuracy while also boosting privacy classification performance. Furthermore, we integrate the graph-based model into a sophisticated multi-fusion network that also processes pixel-based and embedding-based information. Through our approach, we demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing graph-based and traditional multi-fusion models in both privacy classification performance and overall accuracy.

In a recent study, entropy changes were examined for two interacting atoms within an Rabi model featuring an entangled environment, consisting of two coupled cavities. Contrary to the standard Rabi model, the proposed ICI Rabi model features the coupling of each atom to its respective cavity field, along with the entangling of the two cavity fields. The total entropy flow from the combined environment was investigated by analyzing the rate at which entropy is exchanged between the atoms and their surrounding environment. The results indicate that, in the conventional Rabi model, entropy flows in a statistically entangled manner, whereas the entangling environment leads to a total entropy flow that is free from quantum correlations. The proposed ICI Rabi model, however, reveals the fascinating phenomenon of the entropy flow itself becoming quadratically entangled with the environment. Theoretical analysis and numerical computations demonstrate that the quantum entanglement between the atoms is negatively impacted by the entangling environment, but the decay rate actually increases beyond a certain threshold of entropy exchange.

Measurements of central Pb+Pb 2007 GeV/c^2 collisions have revealed, for the first time, a significant difference in the alteration of photon-tagged jets versus inclusive jets. A notable observation is that jets with a preceding photon exhibit greater modification than inclusive jets at low p_T values, with a cross-section ratio that decreases as transverse momentum increases from 30 to 80 GeV/c^2. These results are compared against model predictions from both a hard scattering model and two models of modified transport coefficients for highly energetic particles in a simulated quark-gluon plasma.

The advancement in deep learning has sparked significant interest from theorists and computer scientists in understanding its application to various problems in theoretical and applied mechanics. Furthermore, the evolving hardware landscape is driving a need to re-evaluate the efficiency of computational algorithms through the lens of modern low-precision computing architectures. This talk introduces two innovative methodological approaches - one for solving reverse problems and the other for theoretical analysis of problems involving partial differential equations - both of which leverage the power of computational modeling. Additionally, examples of efficient numerical solutions are presented, utilizing state-of-the-art computational techniques such as deep neural networks and Legendre deep neural space galley methods. These solutions achieve optimal results while adapting to the performance capabilities of cutting-edge computing hardware.

Detecting hard X-rays emitted by the quiet Sun is an ongoing challenge, primarily due to interference from instrumental noise and the influence of the Earth's magnetosphere. By combining high spatial resolution imaging from the Foxsey Image Spectrometer Imager (FOXSI) with precise timing of its orbital crossings, researchers have successfully isolated the quiet Sun's signal from dominant sources of interference. This is achieved by monitoring the quiet Sun during key periods such as magnetospheric orbit insertion, low earth orbit, and pre- and post-sunrise, while accounting for the rotating Earth's varying effect. By analyzing the quiet Sun's brightness in relation to the Sun's disk and active regions, researchers have established the lowest level of the quiet Sun's known X-ray emission and providing the most accurate model of its light source to date.

Determining the degree of user influence within large social networks is a complex and computationally challenging task, especially when graph representations are subject to rapid changes as new information is added. Graph-based methods, which are commonly applied to pinpoint influential users in static datasets, often fail to adapt to dynamic graphs effectively. To address this issue, we propose incorporating augmentation techniques both during training and testing phases to enhance the accuracy of dynamic influence prediction. By generating synthetic user interactions and expanding user sets, we can enable models to generalize better and adapt to new data more efficiently. Our experiments reveal that augmentations are particularly valuable in larger graph datasets, while test-time augmentations offer testing-set specific benefits that training alone cannot provide. To evaluate the accuracy of our approach, we utilized multiple baseline metrics, including user centrality measures, to demonstrate the significant improvement in prediction performance.

Our approach tackles the Euler-Arnold equations, which we reframe as a variational challenge by introducing constraints in the form of natural boundary conditions. Drawing inspiration from this geometric formulation, we develop a straightforward and adaptable numerical technique to tackle complex field theories in quantum field theory. By introducing a versatile and straightforward method, we demonstrate its successful application to various non-linear field theories, including scalar $f(R)$ gravity, $\lambda \phi^4$, and sine-Gordon models in $1+1$ dimensions, yielding novel solutions that exhibit diverse characteristics such as solitons and anti-solitons.

A fundamental issue in sensor fusion pose estimation involves accurately calculating the error covariance. Since sensor errors are interdependent, particularly when errors are drawn from the same error distribution, using error correlations can substantially enhance estimation accuracy. However, properly computing these error correlations often proves difficult. Our research introduces a straightforward technique for modeling error correlations based on stochastic properties of the errors, which enables more accurate pose estimations by taking into account the errors' correlations without the need for filters or estimators. Our experimental findings demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness and efficiency, and its applicability to various error distributions, including complex multivariate cases.

The idea of a multi-temperature universe with varying temperatures across different regions offers a novel framework for studying the scale-dependent behavior of dark matter cross-sections. Our study focuses on the cross-over from the Large Scale Structure (LSS) to (re)collapse epochs, where distinct temperatures exist side by side within the same dark matter field. By combining a simplified analytical model with detailed simulations, we demonstrate that, within this context, the dark matter cross-section can be accurately split into two distinct parts, corresponding to the two coexisting temperature-dependent cross-sections at any given moment. Furthermore, we apply these findings to three distinct dark matter models to analyze the scale-dependent behavior of their dark matter interactions.

An investigation into the production of paired same-sign W bosons was conducted utilizing proton-proton collision data from 13 TeV energy collisions, with a total of 139 fb^-1 luminosity collected by the ATLAS and CMS experiments. The data exhibited a significant excess over standard model predictions, with an observed significance of 3.2 sigma, and this excess was most pronounced in a specific decay channel where two positively charged leptons (electrons or muons) and at least two jets, including a possible jet from a boson decay, are present. An search for the produced particles within model frameworks that include the minimal SU(2) triplet and a complex scalar triplet was also performed, with no exclusion of these models obtained due to the observed data being in contradiction with the model's expectations.

Gray-scale images hold substantial information in terms of pixel connections, which is why they are preferred for use with deep learning models. However, these models demand a substantial amount of data for training, which is difficult to acquire in the case of colored images. Our aim is to train a deep learning model on a gray-scale input image to incorporate the required color details into it. To achieve this, we've developed a novel approach that allows the model to be trained with a smaller set of colored images while still using a large amount of grayscale data to supplement it. Our method involves integrating the model's architecture with two specific components that enable color detail integration and the utilization of grayscale pixel connections, respectively. Our solution's efficiency and colorfulness have been verified through comprehensive evaluations, which demonstrate that it surpasses the efficiency of prior state-of-the-art methods while requiring less trained data.

We analyze the cosmological parameter outcomes from our study using the Planck light curves in the nonlinear $P(q)$ model, which allows for a non-flat universe with $A_L=1$. The Planck data show that this model nearly matches a flat, $\Lambda$CDM universe, but the lack of tension in $\sigma_8$ and $H_0$ suggests it may not fully represent the accelerating dark energy. We now propose a modified version of the $P(q)$ model, consisting of three curves, which measure the cosmological parameters under varying deceleration/acceleration rates from $z=3.4$ to $z=0$. The Planck data reveal that a nearly standard $\Lambda$CDM universe characterizes the early universe, while a more rapidly accelerating dark energy is needed in the recent past. The modified model, which measures the cosmological parameters under varying deceleration/acceleration rates, shows that a nearly standard $\Lambda$CDM universe characterizes the early universe, while a rapidly accelerating dark energy is needed in the recent past. The modified model, which nearly matches a flat, $\Lambda$CDM universe, could be the result of a misunderstanding in analyzing the accelerating dark energy as described by the Planck data, and we suggest a more thorough study into the model's implications on cosmological parameters.

In between releases, a significant number of files experiencing changes are still required for upkeep. Several platforms for collaborative coding track file modifications over time but neglect to monitor maintenance activities on existing files. An in-depth examination of more than 200 software projects reveals that between releases, a substantial proportion of files experiencing changes are slated for upkeep. An analysis into the mechanisms for monitoring maintenance activities shows that, although some repositories utilize automated methods, others rely on manual tracking. As a result, there's a pressing need for a unified, reliable system to monitor maintenance activities across all repositories.

BD And, a binary with components that could be an analog for many close binary stars, shows an unresolved third light source that requires further investigation to confirm, a discovery that could significantly impact our understanding of this system and its study of exoplanets, especially as its potential presence could lead to the conclusion that existing data does not support the existence of a exoplanet in the system.

This research shows that on compact complex surfaces, the Yamabe flow converges towards a stable metric representing a K\"ahler-Einstein condition, provided the initial surface's first Chern class matches that of a K\"ahler-Einstein class. Furthermore, we prove the existence of both periodic and chaotic behavior in the Yamabe flow for certain surfaces.

In modern recommendation systems, multiple negative examples are employed to accelerate model convergence, however, their distribution is often non-uniform, thereby biasing preference learning. We observe that conventional models are ineffective at distinguishing valuable aspect-specific examples from irrelevant ones, thus hindering their adaptability and flexibility. To address this limitation, we propose GaPE, an enhancement for learning user preferences, where aspects can be predetermined or dynamically inferred from interaction patterns. Firstly, our novel GaPE module maintains user representations by selectively incorporating high-quality aspect-specific examples, ultimately improving the accuracy of neighboring user embeddings. Secondly, we devise an entanglement decoder that infers aspects from users' neighboring representations, thereby fostering iterative refinement of aspect and user preference learning. Experimental results show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art models, particularly in covering diverse aspects, thereby offering enhanced recommendations, while also reducing inference cost.

This article applies obstruction theory to compute obstruction spaces within symplectic sheaves. By utilizing this, we can provide an alternative expression for the symplectic sheaf cohomology as a direct limit. In addition, we establish a precise condition under which the obstruction spaces vanish, thereby enabling the calculation of the symplectic cohomology in certain cases. As a result of this analysis, we derive a precise symplectic cohomology description for smooth manifolds possessing a symplectic atlas with linear compatibilities.

To analyze properties of partitions limited by how many times parts can repeat, traditional generating functions often require complicated approaches. This paper introduces a tool called an embedded generating function to simplify and clarify these types of restrictions, allowing for more straightforward derivation of identities. The concept of embedded generating functions builds on similar functions used to track partition frequencies, and it can be adjusted based on the specific repetition rules for parts. Using this tool, we reestablish several known identities, such as those relating to partitions restricted to specific numbers of parts or with a maximum part frequency.

We analyze the stability of function approximation under exact data samples using the weighted least squares method with weights influenced by a prior distribution. Our analysis reveals that with the weighted least squares, we achieve both numerical stability and optimality without relying on regularization. While weights based on a uniform prior lead to suboptimal results, weights based on a Gaussian prior, however, guarantee optimal approximations with a bounded error margin of 1.12 times the optimal result. Our approach also encompasses certain interpolation methods, such as the weighted average of function values, which works effectively for functions that are nearly constant. Likewise, we examine a mimicry method that minimizes the maximum possible error, which gives rise to nonnegative weights but may result in worse performance due to the absence of optimality guarantees.

In analogy to the Kondo model, we have developed a Fock space mapping for tight-binding chains with randomly varying site energies, influenced by nearest-neighbor site interactions. Initially, this method is applied to develop an exact full configuration interaction (FCI) approach to systematically study the impact of these specific interactions on the system's low-energy, localized states, specifically focusing on the Delocalization Transition in disordered semiconductor systems like Si:P. By self-consistently including the most significant configuration interactions within the Fock space, this new "Kondo-like" model is able to provide a more accurate representation of the localized states localized in such systems. To an extent, certain configuration interactions in this model mimic the well-known behavior associated with the Fock space mapping of the Anderson model, where a local magnetic moment is formed through the configuration interactions of a single electron localized on a lattice site, as localized in a Fock space, similar to the system of the Anderson model itself. Nonetheless, certain configuration interactions in this model are able to produce more complex localized states within the system, specifically those involving the simultaneous occupation of multiple adjacent lattice sites, such as the local dipolar, tri-polar, and more localized states localized in the system, specifically those localized in a Fock space, similar to the system of the Anderson model itself. This model is specifically designed to study the Delocalization Transition in disordered semiconductor systems like Si:P, and certain other phenomena of interest in such systems.

Generalized standard OGS for the finite classical Coxeter group of type B_n are represented by 6-tuples with bounded entries. The paper focuses on exchanging laws within these tuples and reveals their connection to the generalized standard OGS properties of position and sign. Specifically, the paper is concerned with exchanging the absolute values or signs of adjacent entries in a given tuple. The study's findings demonstrate that the generalized standard OGS for B_n are connected through specific equations involving the tuple elements. Furthermore, the paper is related to a generalized type B sinusoidal sum formula, extending Sun's work, and also considers special cases corresponding to van der Corput sequence sign sums and van der Corput sequence sinusoidal sums.

In scalar field theories with SU(N) x U(1) symmetry, coupled to SU(N) gauge fields and defined in an SU(N) symmetric random matrix vacuum, we investigate the effects of SU(N) gauge dynamics and U(1) symmetry breaking on each other. Although the SU(N) gauge dynamics inherently preserve the U(1) current, both the gauge field and symmetry breaking can in principle affect the U(1) current's divergence. By computing the divergence of the U(1) current, we demonstrate that finite SU(N) gauge dynamics do not break U(1) symmetry explicitly. Furthermore, we have developed an explicit gauge fixing procedure that maintains unitary gauge without influencing gauge dynamics, confirming that both SU(N) gauge dynamics and U(1) symmetry can be simultaneously implemented in this framework.

This research introduces a transparent and topologically precise framework for robot learning in dynamic real-world settings. By integrating hierarchical Bayesian modeling with directed graph analysis, our model predicts potential distractions and models task-irrelevant elements. As a result, this hierarchical approach allows robots to acquire diverse task-related patterns while maintaining consistency across multiple tasks. To validate the model's principles and practical application, we provide an empirical analysis examining various topological patterns within directed graphs, along with a detailed case study of a mobile robot successfully navigating through multiple activities including driving, charging, and interacting with other robots.

The whisker topology on a space X creates a local, Hausdorff group topology with base $\Whis{X}$ consisting of sets that exclude certain points from a translation. Research has shown that the whisker topology can be used to classify spaces up to continuous maps, allowing for the analysis of the resulting quotient space $X/\!\!\!\!\!\relax_{w}$, known as the Weser quotient space. Our first key finding demonstrates that the whisker and lasso topologies on $X/\!\!\!\!\!\relax_{w}$ coincide if X has a single non-trivial orbit and its non-trivial components are closed under isotopy-invariant unions. Furthermore, we establish a criterion for X to have a weakly semilocal uniform structure, requiring the existence of a closed, isotopy-invariant component $C$ with points having compact neighborhoods in $\Whis{C}$.

In contrast to deep reinforcement learning, which relies on random exploration, motion planning is utilized, leveraging specialized motion planners to gather informative experience for learning control policies. A novel framework integrates motion planning into the reinforcement learning process, utilizing a collaborative multi-agent system to streamline the planning and control learning procedures. This framework consists of two key components - a motion planner that gathers experience through simulation, and a controller that refines its actions to maximize rewards, with both working together to maximize long-term rewards. The experience plotters work in harmony with the controller, using a collaborative approach to motion planning to gather diverse trajectories for learning state transitions. The experiment demonstrates the framework's effectiveness in solving a complex 3D maze navigation task, exhibiting faster convergence, enhanced exploration, and superior performance, compared to reinforcement learning with motion planning, while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to methods without motion planning in production.

Our study explores gas disk accretion onto a cluster of growing black holes (CBHs) at the heart of galaxies. Using the SBHcode simulation, which models the evolution of CBHs alongside stellar systems, we find that CB growth through Eddington-type gas disk accretion lags behind typical star formation timescales by a factor of 2 to 3. By incorporating CB growth and its impact on the CB dynamical evolution, we observe an accelerated CB speed-up. At approximately 300 million years after onset, individual black holes reach masses of about 10^7-10^8 M_\odot. Near the end of simulations, most cluster cores become dynamically unstable, causing black holes to merge and reducing the number of CBHs. Ultimately, only one central supermassive black hole remains. In most cases, the SMBH ends up with a mass of about 10^8 M_\odot. Our research indicates that in galaxy formation processes, early stages of growth are dominated by growth of individual black holes, while later stages see the rapid increase of the SMBH through mergers.

To effectively leverage big data, deep learning methods have been widely adopted, but their final outcomes often lack clarity due to their intricate nature. UNCURE, a novel probabilistic deep learning approach introduced in this paper, utilizes a Bayesian neural network setup to accurately quantify uncertainty in deeply learned features, thereby reducing the uncertainty in their upstream classification results. By integrating UNCURE's uncertainty quantification into a deeply learned feature extraction and classification pipeline, it enhances the transparency and reliability of these upstream outcomes. In our experiments, UNCURE achieved superior accuracy rates of 97.4% and 97% on two prominent blood cancer datasets, outperforming established uncertainty quantification methods by 1-2% in accuracy rates.

Researchers analyzing trends in neuroscience publications combined both preprints and published articles along with citation data to investigate the impact of preprints on neuroscience. To achieve this, they collaborated with multiple neuroscience journals and preprint servers to gather publication data, then used an automated method to scrape and organize associated metadata and abstracts. Subsequent analysis of this combined preprint and publication data along with associated citation counts revealed that preprints accelerate the typical publication timeline by 3-4 months, while also increasing publication citation rates. However, it was found that the practice of citing preprints wanes more rapidly than the practice of citing published articles.

This paper explores a computational method to automatically generate electronic lab notebooks, inspired by the tradition of handwritten lab records. As electronic lab notebooks accumulate data, traditional methods become cumbersome and prone to errors due to missing自动化管理. In response, a modular framework is proposed to automate data integration from diverse sources, produce a coherent document, and facilitate collaboration among researchers. Implementing this system has shown significant data management improvements, including reduced human error, enhanced data consistency, and increased researcher collaboration.

To accelerate the development of advanced materials for specific purposes, it's crucial to master the process of material design and modification to achieve desired properties. Researchers have been working on developing predictive models using machine learning and statistical methods to forecast material formations, mechanical properties, and more, but these methods come with limitations in understanding complex relationships and requiring significant computational resources. This study presents a new, efficient approach that integrates quantitative structure-property relationships (QSPR) with evolutionary optimizations and uncertainty estimations to efficiently develop high-performance materials. Focusing on data-driven design, this approach is verified using experimental data from single-crystal nickel-based superalloys, revealing how increasing the complexity of crystallographic features in their microstructures significantly improves mechanical performance at low temperatures and increases the durability at higher temperatures. Furthermore, the uncertainty analysis verifies the reliability of the discovered structure-property relationships, and the developed models can create quantitative and qualitative criteria for selecting optimal material features, contributing to the development of precise materials for various applications, such as cold-environment materials and heat-resistant materials.

Initial research has shown that whether the heavy doubly charmed baryon $T_{cc}^+$ or the heavier, charged baryon $T_{cc}^{*+}$ can exist as stable particles that lie below their respective decay products in mass is irrelevant in examining the possible strong interaction between them. Since both $T_{cc}^+$ and $T_{cc}^{*+}$ are highly desirable targets for potential discovery at the LHC, understanding their decay processes and final state interactions is a crucial prerequisite. Given that their production mechanisms are quite limited and result in low yields, the primary production method for these particles will be $D^{\tau}D$ and $D^{\tau}\tau$ decays of the $D_s^\pm$ meson. With the aim of exploring $T_{cc}^{*\pm}$'s possibility, a $T_{cc}^{+\tau^-}$, which was previously unexamined, has been investigated for the $T_{cc}^{*+}$, via $D_s^\pm T_{cc}^{+\tau^-}$, as well as by analyzing $D_s^\pm T_{cc}^{*\pm}$, via $D_s^\pm T_{cc}^{*\tau^-}$ and $D_s^\pm T_{cc}^{*\tau^+}$, within the framework in which both $T_{cc}^+$ and $T_{cc}^{*

Recent advancements in machine learning have enabled graph neural networks to create subspaces for grouping similar data, which has shown great potential in solving the clustering problem, especially when dealing with noisy or incomplete data. Leveraging this concept, we introduce a novel approach called semantic clustering, which addresses a broader clustering problem that encompasses traditional clustering methods. We develop a framework that formulates a mathematical optimization problem and utilize graph neural networks to train low-dimensional representations, capturing various occlusion levels. By applying this framework to the semantic clustering task, we achieve effective results on the NPSITCB dataset from NIPS-2019, demonstrating the potential of the approach in the field of computer science.

This project undertakes an exploration of completeness problems in classic combinatorial areas, beginning with a focus on properties of hyperbolas and ellipses in a defined geometric context. We establish methods for identifying whether hyperbolic curves and elliptical curves in specific configurations form complete sets based on their Sideteness properties. Furthermore, this analysis extends to encompass similar properties in the infinite version of these geometric configurations.

In our previous research on diverse sampling, various methods employed a binary matrix to measure the diversity of sampled objects, with non-zero entries indicating the influence of previous samples on the likelihood of selecting new ones. Our most recent approach revealed the power of leveraging a non-uniform distribution to improve sampling efficiency. This paper builds upon that work, offering two key advancements. Firstly, we developed theoretical bounds analogous to those of uniform sampling, but significantly tighter due to the non-uniform probability usage, where the improvement is directly proportional to the ratios of probabilities involved. Secondly, we introduced an optimized non-uniform sampling algorithm, eliminating the need for matrix updates and leveraging a pre-computed binary matrix to enhance computation speed. Notably, our modified approach still satisfies the desired diversity constraints. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets have verified the effectiveness of our sampling methods.

The DGLAP schema, which governs the scale-dependent behavior of parton distribution functions, is utilized in PDFs fits to transition between different QCD scales and match theoretical models experimental data. This paper investigates whether employing next-to-leading order (NLO) or next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) PDFs impacts the evolution outcome when starting from NLO or NNLO QCD calculations, and how this affects the analysis interpretation. Calculations were conducted using ANNLO and NNLOQCD data as well as NNLO and NLO PDFs.
