Machine learning models that adapt to specific tasks by adjusting their configurations are becoming increasingly relevant in generating complex, real-world data, including subatomic particle data. By integrating symmetries into these models, researchers aim to enhance their efficiency by reducing the number of necessary transformations. Nonetheless, a systematic method for building symmetrical neural networks, including those based on normalizing flows, has yet to be established. In this study, we introduce a novel approach for constructing U(1) gauge theories within the framework of normalizing flows, develop gauged normalizing flows, and apply these to distinguish between electrons and positrons. We take significant steps towards the development of a general method for building gauge-invariant normalizing flows.

This research focuses on developing biased recognition systems that enhance the accuracy of text identification when specific formats are anticipated. Unlike existing methods, which typically focus on meeting format expectations post-hoc, our systems integrate these expectations into the model for real-time biasing. Both word-level and character-level approaches were tested on curated datasets that simulate various well-known text identifiers, such as email addresses and phone numbers, and our results indicate that biasing can significantly improve accuracy in identifying text information.

This report presents initial results from a top quark pair cross-section measurement using 8 TeV proton-proton collision data, collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 20.3 fb-1. The cross-section was determined using a matrix element cross-section of 6.034 ± 0.113 (stat.) ± 0.115 (syst.) nb, which was found to be in agreement with predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics at next-to-next-to-leading order combined with next-to-leading log corrections. The cross-section was further found to be in accordance with predictions from the standard model.

Machine learning techniques have been increasingly integrated with advanced processor pipelines to boost execution precision, yet their effectiveness is often compromised in scenarios where a database is absent or contains irrelevant information. A novel execution framework has been developed to mitigate these adverse effects by optimizing processor-out memory access efficiency. By predicting the contents of external machines and refining execution outcomes based on that anticipation, this framework significantly reduces the magnitude of discrepancies in output data. Furthermore, its efficiency is enhanced through parameter refinement using database historical data, thereby minimizing the reliance on flawed predictions and data inaccuracies. Notably, our framework has demonstrated remarkable accuracy improvements of up to 60% compared to a baseline processor-out memory access model, with an average reduction of data inaccuracies by a factor of two.

We analyze the angle correlations between galaxies found in the Low Frequency Array Sky Survey pilot project to learn more about the distribution of mass at a specific depth of 1.38 GHz. By utilizing the $w_{\rm L}$ and $w_{p0}$ parameters from a series of fitting processes, we compare our findings to those predicted by the $\Lambda$CDM model, taking into account the power spectrum of the matter distribution defined by the year-2020 problem definition for cosmic systematics. A $\chi^2$ analysis of the statistical behavior of the parameters reveals that they are consistently aligned with the $\Lambda$CDM model, presenting a tension of about 1.9 standard deviations in the value of the parameters that reflect the slope of the power spectrum, and power normalized at 8 megaparsecs/h, respectively, with systematic factors that could be influencing the result to a similar extent. Furthermore, we explore the effectiveness of a series of theoretical scenarios that could be influencing the angle correlations of the galaxies and discuss the variety of statistics that could be employed to constrain the angle correlations of galaxies to define more precisely the evolution of the cosmic system over time.

The Lasso problem with constraints imposed by the rank is computationally challenging due to its difficult structure, despite having a convex formulation. A proposed algorithm, based on adaptive sieving methods, efficiently tackles this high-dimensional Lasso problem, particularly in the context of panel data econometrics, where it can identify heterogeneous effects across multiple dimensions. By utilizing an approach that exponentially reduces the number of variables to optimize in the primal problem and employing a gradient descent method with a learning rate adjusted according to problem conditions, this algorithm achieves polynomial-time complexity. Numerical tests confirm its effectiveness even with severe rank constraints and in the presence of rank-related constraints in the dual problem.

Building upon earlier findings that only the initial and final states of a system and its environment matter for calculating the entropy production rate (EEP), this study demonstrates through a thorough analysis of optimal protocols for reaching equilibrium that a unique global optimal method exists in this context. The necessity and validity of this optimal protocol have been verified across various theoretical and practical examples, encompassing both classical and quantum systems. The concept of this optimal protocol has significant implications in the analysis of the maximum work that can be obtained from stochastic thermal processes.

To mitigate the environmental impact of their AI services, organizations need a method to measure the environmental burden of their AI workloads. Our proposal incorporates life cycle assessment (LCA) into existing carbon footprinting approaches, enabling the evaluation of an AI service's entire life cycle, from development to deployment and eventual replacement. To accomplish this, we've integrated LCAs of various computing hardware and data center facilities, allowing for the calculation of emissions associated with training, testing, and running AI models. Additionally, we've developed a life cycle function point method to determine the code segments required for model operations, facilitating the estimation of setup and running costs. Furthermore, we've explored the integration of renewable energy and green credits into our lifecycle modeling to account for sustainable power sources. By applying our framework to a popular image classification model, we've highlighted its ability to identify differences in efficiency and guide users toward more sustainable AI model choices.

Prescriptive process monitoring method development often relies on simulated data, yet to truly assess the methods' effectiveness, experimentation must occur in actual processes. A proposed framework assesses the efficacy of PPM methods in two real-world contexts, enabling researchers to test and compare their performance on live data before deploying them in practice.

To solve the coupled problem of Darcy-forced convection, we employ a continuous finite element method using two spaces in the primal formulation. This approach is validated by the inf-sup condition. Furthermore, we apply the duality-weighted residual method for error estimation and its application for solution improvement. Experimental results also explore the optimal estimation of errors without adaptation.

Graph packing problems, specifically those involving vertex-disjoint paths, are notoriously difficult to solve with tight bounds. Although lower bounds can be easily obtained using a linear programming relaxation called the fractional relaxation, the same cannot be said for integral solutions. Consequently, the integrality gap of such path packings has remained elusive to precisely define. In this work, a simple and efficient algorithm is proposed that provides a (1+O(log log n)/log n) approximation for the maximum number of K_r-free path packings in an n-vertex graph, improving upon previous results which had only achieved an O(log n) gap.

This study explores the formation of socially distinct groups, or cliques, in opinions that can be measured quantitatively, such as temperature settings in households. By adapting a one-dimensional Ising model to represent opinions, where neighbors strive to minimize differences, the dynamics of the system give rise to unique social structures. Through theoretical analysis and computer simulations, it's demonstrated that cliques emerge with specific width and abundance patterns. Notably, the majority of cliques are small in size, with few large groups, mirroring observations in real-world social structures. Furthermore, interventions aiming to merge adjacent cliques often necessitate a significant shift in one clique's opinion, suggesting the robustness of these social distinct groups.

We investigate a previously underexplored branch in Einstein-Klein-Gordon model parameter space characterized by two key variables: the gravitational potential at infinity and the coefficient of the black hole's mass term in the Klein-Gordon equation. Our analysis focuses on extremal Reissner-Nordström black holes to identify solutions featuring hair, which we achieve by modifying the Klein-Gordon equation with an additional mass term. This parameter space is vast, yet it includes areas that directly correspond with holographic superconductors. Notably, our model's solutions with matching characteristics as previously established holographic superconducting black holes also exhibit a critical temperature dependence mirroring that of those solutions. This finding adds credibility to our model's potential to offer a theoretical framework for further exploring holographic superconductors through more general scalar fields.

Our understanding of the early stages of gene expression has been limited due to the inability to distinguish between intermediate forms of nascent RNA. Recent advancements using methods like MAXI-seq overcome this challenge by providing high-resolution sequencing data that can be used to create models predicting the time lag between finished transcription and the production of mature mRNA in eukaryotic genes. By extending these principles to random sequences and incorporating variability in transcription rates, first passage times can be calculated, which aligns well with experimental observations of RNA accumulation in yeast cells for specific genes.

High-energy $\alpha$-decay data have been analyzed for $^{64}$Ni, yielding energy levels up to 6 MeV in a detailed spectrum for the first time. Nuclear shell model calculations were carried out using the latest interactions to investigate subshell gaps near neutron number 40, focusing on the evolution of these gaps, and using this structure to examine higher multipole transitions. The calculated properties were compared to observed $\alpha$-decay half-lives in order to constrain the nature of the monopole interaction. Notably, there appears to be an unusually robust deformation driving effect influencing both nuclear structure and the property under examination. The study has been compared to observed energy levels and properties of excited states in $^{63}$Ni generated via neutron capture, revealing that even very neutron-rich nuclei exhibit rich and complex high-energy excited state structures.

The fundamental representations of SU(N) gauge theories consist of N fundamental Weyl fermions and a single gluon, whereas the adjoint representation, used in SU(N) gauge theories, includes N^2-1 Weyl fermions and a different number of gluons, leading to differing anomalies. The purpose of this paper is to establish the duality between SU(N) gauge theories utilizing the fundamental and adjoint representations under specific conditions, and within a specific range of coupling.

A recent study by Gullion and Williams investigated the connections between a linear code $C$, its subgroup code $D$, and its dual $D^\perp$, all within a finite abelian group $(G,+)$. This paper builds upon their work by exploring the relationship between the group codes $C$ and $D$ and their dual $D^\perp$. Similarly, the connections between the code $C^\perp$ and its subgroup code $D^\perp$ with their duals $D$ are examined. We demonstrate that the length of a linear code is equivalent to the rank of its subgroup code combined with the index of its subgroup code within the code's parent group $(G,+)$. This equivalence holds for all abelian codes $C$, its subgroup code $D$, and their duals $C^\perp$.

Our work is grounded in a fundamental algorithm, Bucket Elimination, a form of
inference and optimization on an expanded version of undirected Bayesian networks known as
undirected message passing systems. By leveraging this principle, we develop enhanced 
algorithms for specific problem classes by manipulating it in innovative ways. These 
redesigns allow us to perform more efficient and accurate computations. In particular,
we achieve faster optimization methods for basic energy functions and increase the 
accuracy of finding optimal solutions for complex constraint networks. Additionally, we 
obtain a more efficient algorithm for exact marginal calculation in general Markov Random Fields.

To recover from a dropped object interaction, the visual system must integrate information from multiple sources to locate the object. Since fast movements blur the image, individual frames contain limited information, making it essential to incorporate information about the object's motion characteristics. We establish a connection between the dynamics of moving objects and their visual patterns, blending movement data with the visual information in the proposed method. By training an network that takes into account motion blur, it successfully merges information across multiple video frames to identify objects moving at various speeds. This novel approach outperforms current state-of-the-art models, demonstrating robustness against the variations in object motion. Furthermore, by designing a specific evaluation protocol, it validates that integrating information at various temporal scales aligns with how the human eye processes moving objects.

Continuing our investigation into the universality of isotropic jamming, we contrasted the jamming transitions in frictionless and friction-bearing materials, both under isotropic compression and compact shear protocols, via computer simulations and experimental tests using granular particles and social insects. We found that the critical exponents for frictionless compact shear jamming matched isotropic compression, but both the friction-bearing models and experiments exhibited distinct non-universal behavior, which could not be predicted from the compression data. This led us to explore various model features that might be the cause of this discrepancy, such as rotational degrees of freedom, long-range interactions, polydispersity, friction, and noise, but we found that none of these attributes produced different outcomes that could be analogous to compression, thus we proposed that there is an inherent inherent anisotropy in friction-bearing jamming that is unique to the shear protocol, and thus we posited that there is a fundamental distinction between frictionless and friction-bearing jamming transitions.

This study introduces the multiscale model with arithmetic errors, denoted as MS(2)-AR(4), as an approach to model stochastic loads at multiple time scales in complex systems like electricity grids with considerable renewable energy sources. Without this model, incorporating stochastic loads at multiple time scales would necessitate an excessively detailed discrete-time model. In contrast, the MS(2)-AR(4) model can model the loads at two time steps (intra-hourly and inter-hourly) using the terms of just one longer time step. It is derived using operator factorization of a general discrete-time stochastic process. Based on existing literature, the stochastic process is typically assumed to follow an moving average or Markov property, or be induced by a hidden Markov process. An alternative approach is to use existing time series models, such as the well-established autoregressive model, in combination with the arithmetic errors, to make the model simpler and more flexible. The effectiveness and advantages of the proposed model are demonstrated by simulating a mixture of step loads and the analysis of real data from a German sub-transmission node in 2019. The results show that the MS(2)-AR(4) model performs as well as or better than the standard AR model when performance is evaluated using prediction accuracy, load spectrum matching, and parameter parsimony.

Professionals working closely with government-related data governance should be well-informed about algorithmic biases present in Web search outcomes. Although existing research extensively covers Web search biases, the findings are often scattered and dispersed. Therefore, a comprehensive and systematic synthesis of existing literature is essential for professional experts working within data-related data governance. As a result, a substantial meta-review was conducted, leveraging an automated approach for unbiased article selection and manual examination for intricate details. The overarching objective was to offer a thorough and extensive understanding of algorithmic biases present in Web search outcomes. The authors reviewed 92 studies and identified 16 key categories, exploring the biases associated with professional relevance to government-related data governance. Additionally, the risks posed to public governance decision-making processes are discussed along with potential GDDR actions that can be taken to mitigate these risks.

Our research introduces a novel, practical framework for program synthesis that operates quickly and efficiently, even in the program synthesis framework. The framework designs circuits to achieve desired behaviors without any errors, even when the input varies. The framework's efficiency is its key advantage, as it can average less than a second for common tasks, such as converting a decimal number to binary format in under 30 seconds on a standard laptop. The framework's effectiveness was further demonstrated through a series of experiments, as well as applications in real-world problems, such as the SafeMath library in the Ethereum protocol. The framework's design emphasizes the importance of creating a abstract graph, converting it to a concrete circuit, and using a hierarchical, modular design pattern. The framework's capabilities and limitations are summarized in this report.

Climate modeling involves solving complex systems of differential equations, and over the years, various reduction methods have been developed and applied to these models to facilitate more efficient dynamics analysis, identification of parameter influences, and others. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the approaches used in climate model reduction, covering numerical and asymptotic techniques as well as the principles guiding their selection.

Gravitational wave events that trigger stellar mergers and mergers can produce distinctive features in fine structure lines at infrared frequencies, including those at 5.2 micrometers and 7.5 micrometers, on kilonovae. This study examines the potential of future telescopes, such as the Extremely Large Telescope and the Space Wide Field infrared Telescope, to detect these features in infrared spectra of kilonovae following a gravitational wave event. The analysis indicates that these new observatories will have the capability to identify the fine structure lines in infrared on kilonovae under various scenarios, in contrast to earlier telescopes, such as Hubble, which found it difficult to detect these features. The unique detection of these fine structure lines in infrared would help us better understand the physical properties of the kilonovae ejecta and the explosion mechanisms behind them.

In radiation oncology, patients receive therapeutic X-rays to target and destroy cancer, but this process poses challenges in avoiding damage to surrounding healthy tissue, particularly since patients must undergo treatment multiple times for a total dose delivery of up to 60 Gy.  X-ray beams are aimed through multiple windows or openings that allow staff to monitor treatment progress, but this can result in unnecessary staff exposure to X-rays due to misalignments or equipment malfunctions, leading to leaks or spills of X-rays.  Current detectors only emit an audible alert when X-rays are unexpectedly detected, emitting high decibel levels near life-sensitive organs like the ears, which can cause discomfort and distract the operator during treatment.  To address these issues, researchers have proposed developing ergonomic and smart X-ray detectors that reduce staff exposure to X-rays by utilizing haptic feedback to provide tactile alerts as an alternative to audible alerts, integrated with artificial intelligence to detect and prioritize beam leaks.  AI will analyze data patterns to identify the cause of the interruption and prioritize staff safety by notifying the treatment team of the detected issue.

In compositional data analysis, we investigate the behavior of the log-ratio transformation on high-dimensional data that includes zero values. To better understand this, we examine the corresponding computationally feasible closed-form approximations. Both the theoretical log-ratio transformation and the practical approximations are seen to converge in distribution as the dimensionality of the data increases. We also developed a computationally efficient method to calculate the moment generating function of the log-ratio transformation, along with an application to the compositional ANOVA test in the high-dimensional setting. The test compares the discriminative power of the central logratios to a reference density that belongs to a multivariate normal family, thus offering insights into the overall structure of the composition. The test's empirical performance in the high-dimensional setting is also demonstrated through simulation.

The current understanding of planet formation through core accretion needs improvement, particularly in the area of the predictions regarding mass, final host star distances, and age distributions of large planets. A significant discrepancy exists between theoretical predictions of runaway gas accretion zones and observed exoplanet Haul, with a potential resolution by considering variations in the disk gas mass and temperature structures. This could imply that certain large planets formed in the inner regions beyond typical zones for gas accretion. Moreover, there are few small-mass planets found close to their host stars with masses greater than 10 Earth masses. This suggests that another planet formation process, which is not clear at the moment, forms planetary cores that migrate inward.

A novel neural architecture for predictive agents is developed, featuring reflective capabilities and adaptive memory system to monitor hidden states that drive state transitions. The agent, which operates on partial observations, utilizes its memory to track unmaskable states, as changes in shared memory often correlate with changes in unseeable states. The resulting agent model, enabled by simple back-propagation training, exhibits superior performance in tracking hidden states, minimizing prediction errors on seeable state transitions, as demonstrated in controlled training and testing scenarios. The implementation, including agent architecture, two testing environments, and training code, is publicly accessible.

Constraints are set on a particular dark matter model, involving the absorption of a scalar mediator by dark matter in an s-wave manner, through a combination of direct detection experiments and astrophysical observations of the Sun and Galactic center. Significant limitations are placed on the interaction between the mediator and dark matter when the mediator is much lighter than the dark matter, regardless of whether certain resonance conditions are met. In contrast, when the mediator and dark matter masses are comparable, a wide range of dark matter masses are excluded, with the medium-strength interaction typically yielding the most stringent limits.

Evaluating an individual's cognitive capacity requires examining their ability to handle multiple tasks simultaneously. Traditionally, researchers have used sets of tasks that do not fully capture multi-task interaction due to their focus on single tasks in isolation. To address this, a new study introduces Mod-Cog, an expanded set of 120 tasks with 18 baseline activities, offering insights into multi-task complexity, variety, and flexibility. By applying a statistical approach to analyze task interactions, the study not only confirms existing findings but also identifies novel connections. Additionally, the study employs a multilayer neural network to predict individual performance and uses this approach to guide the creation of customized task sets. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for developing precise and adaptable systems to assess and train various cognitive skills.

We investigate the structure of geometric varieties associated with nilpotent algebra types, giving particular attention to nilpotent Lie algebras and commutative algebras. We establish a connection between an algebra's irreducibility properties and its dimension or Malcev rank in various algebra types. Furthermore, we introduce a method for decomposing geometric varieties into distinct prime components, enabling a more precise analysis of their structure. This new understanding allows us to determine all maximal dimensional geometric varieties for nilpotent Lie algebras and classify those of dimension one for commutative algebras.

The vast, radiative jets extending from supermassive black holes are primarily result of relativistic electrons interacting with photons from the Cosmic Microwave Background via the Inverse Compton effect, making this process a crucial component in understanding the radiation of the jets. The electrons constituting the jets are believed to originate from the black hole, but their exact formation process remains a topic of discussion. Some theories suggest a conductive electrical connection between a rotating black hole and its surrounding disk, whereas other research indicates a turbulent motion, induced by the hydrodynamic instability of the disk, capable of generating the required currents. By utilizing detailed simulations of black hole magnetosphere and disk dynamics, and applying relativistic magnetohydrodynamic equations, we are able to model the electron distribution within the jets and calculate the resulting radiation from the Cosmic Microwave background, thereby gaining insight into the origin of the radiation observed in the jets.

To achieve an analytical post-Newtonian expansion in general relativity, the 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization leverages a unique Fock-Schwartz gauge that simplifies the expansion process. By using a common cosmological notation for the weak-field limit, we can make a direct and well-documented post-Newtonian expansion from the Einstein field equations, Levier-Schwarzschild solution, and (Schutz) Scherrwarzschild initial data. As we move to higher orders, increasing post-Newtonian orders, the 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization exhibits greater advantages due to its fixed gauge freedom, in contrast to the standard PN gauge, which requires a change in coordinates to maintain consistency.

This research presents a novel method for image registration called SIFT feature point matching combined with geometric transformation, specifically designed to perform robustly in medical whole-body MRI scans. The method employs the Oriented Gradient Flow technique to establish consistent image feature correspondence and encompasses a global image transformation model to avoid local divergence. By incorporating the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) descriptor, the proposed approach enables reliable descriptor matching across a variety of image variations, including differences in orientation, size, intensity, and local irregularities. Furthermore, the algorithm incorporates the principle of information mutual dependence to optimize the transformation model and achieve a precise fit by minimizing the distance between images. Evaluation through the registration of whole-body MRI scans demonstrates the proposed SIFT-CPD method's robust performance in terms of target accuracy and processing efficiency, and its suitability for application in medical image preprocessing and automatic segmentation.

We use several years' worth of precise astrometric data from NASA's TESS satellite to study a changing binary star system consisting of two white dwarfs that eclipses each other and exhibits a unique period variation pattern of about 8 years consisting of consecutive accelerating and decelerating phases. This phenomenon in the system J082239.54$+$304857.19 can be explained by the presence of an unseen third star interacting gravitationally and causing the observed astrometric shifts, similar to a previously similar system of J002244.84$+$304429.06 but with key differences such as the two visible white dwarfs in the former system interacting with three bodies, whereas the latter system typically consists of just one visible white dwarf surrounded by two interacting stars. Our analysis suggests that the two visible white dwarfs in the system J082239.54$+$304857.19 have similar masses of approximately 0.4 solar mass, while the unseen interacting star has a more massive 0.75 solar mass configuration, possibly an object nearing the Chandrasekhar limit or potentially a rapidly spinning sub-Chandrasekhar mass object or a unique type of helium-core white dwarf rotating near its maximum speed due to its synchrotron emission characteristics.

To limit the growth in the number of parameters and computational complexity of
a deep learning model, particularly after increasing its depth, we have developed a
universal optimal transport-based pooling framework that can be applied across
different pooling methods to enhance their performance. By incorporating an UT
module in each pooling layer, allowing for a flexible redefinition of the cost
function to measure feature representation disparities between input and output
features, an adjustable transport cost is determined, leading to an improved
model convergence, accuracy, and efficiency. Experimental findings illustrate
the effectiveness of our proposed method with consistent results across various
scenarios and datasets, and we provide modified versions of different pooling
operators for use within our framework. Furthermore, we present an ideal unified
framework for pooling operator design.

We conducted an in-depth study of 166 spiral galaxies from the SDSS database, each hosting a Seyfert nucleus of either type 1 or 2, focusing on establishing nuclear orientation distributions. By comparing the nuclear orientation within a specific set of database-selected Seyfert galaxies, our analysis yielded several key findings. Firstly, we discovered that type 1 and type 2 Seyfert nuclei are not evenly distributed within their host galaxies but are instead tilted towards aligning with the galaxy's disk. Secondly, we established that type 2 Seyfert nuclei demonstrate a more pronounced alignment with their galaxy's disk compared to type 1 Seyfert nuclei, with the former exhibiting a more distinct non-random orientation distribution. Moreover, our research provided evidence that both Seyfert types are more likely to be found in edge-on galaxy orientations than in face-on ones, with the effect of the alignment more pronounced in type 2 Seyfert nuclei. Notably, our analysis did not reveal a correlation between the galaxies' disk inclination and the ratio of type 2 to type 1 Seyfert nuclei. Furthermore, our research did not reveal a connection between the nuclear hardness of the Seyfert nuclei and the effect of the alignment with the galaxy's disk. Lastly, our analysis did not reveal a connection between the nuclear orientation within a particular set of galaxies and their distance from the galaxy's center, either in terms of angular kiloparsecs or in terms of the logarithmic surface brightness of the galaxy's disk. This research presents a characterization of flat general rotational surfaces in Lorentzian space $\mathbb{S}^2_1$ via their pointwise 1-gauss maps, followed by an examination of submanifolds in this same space that share specific 1-gauss maps with prescribed parallel directions.

While labs are commonly taught how to set up controlled experiments, using science as a model for AI pre-training has received less attention. This course provides a different approach to AI pre-training by leveraging easily obtainable data - students' observations of their surroundings - and demonstrating that this data has substantial value for learning general AI skills. Instead of relying on conventional image classification, we suggest using geometry estimation as the starting point for pre-training, due to its potential for providing more transferable skills and being prioritized by the estimation of the environment's layout. This can lead to the development of image understanding models capable of producing accurate 3D reconstructions and generating corresponding 2D representations. Our proposal leverages an efficient estimator that can process large amounts of data within a single GPU day using modern deep learning architectures. We utilize this model to pre-train a flexible transformer-based renderer on varied tasks with minimal additional parameters. The course teaches how to set up this approach on a diverse range of devices and collect relevant data.

Time-series data is prevalent in various industries, including finance and healthcare. However, obtaining accurately annotated training data for TCube's use is a complex and time-consuming process, limiting its practical application. To address this challenge, we introduce TCube, a Time-series Cuboid-Based event representation scheme that facilitates modeling temporal patterns in events. TCube's use of high-cardinality categorical variables enables discovering correlations without relying on extensive training data, making it a novel and effective feature extraction method for time-series events. We evaluated TCube's efficacy by comparing its outcomes with event-based and traditional features, revealing significant improvements of up to 10 and 15% in logistic regression models, respectively. To showcase TCube's applicability, we implemented it in an ordered book inventory system, where it enabled using the book return event for predicting the exercise event,发现 both positive and negative correlations between the two events.

We have placed new limits on the significance of standard model effective field coefficients coupling to the $b\mu+\mu-$ interaction, specifically considering the $B^0_s\to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays, the latter of which is previously unobserved. These constraints are derived from the latest measurements of the $B^0_s\to \mu^+\mu-$ decay, and by incorporating previously unobserved $B^0\to \mu^+\mu-$ observation, alongside considering theoretical uncertainties in hadronic processes. These constraints are then used to evaluate the impact on the charged Higgs in two-Higgs-doublet and general two-Higgs-doublet models, particularly in relation to charged Higgs contributions to anomalous magnetic moments of the $b$ quark and the $\mu$on, and to $B^0_s\to \mu^+\mu-$ decay. Our investigation demonstrates that in general two-Higgs-doublet models, the charged Higgs mass is constrained to be below the $1$ TeV range by present data, a limitation that is further strengthened when considering future high-luminosity data at the LHC, especially for $B^0\to \mu^+\mu-$ decay, which is predicted to be observable in the near future.

Using the Ising model on a Cayley tree based on the free group F(n), we develop a transfer matrix method utilizing features of the tree's inherent tree-like structure and symmetric properties of the Ising model. This method yields a novel, reduced-dimensional transfer matrix of size 2^n on a set of functions derived from the powers of the Cauchy integral over a unit disk. We demonstrate the correctness of this approach by establishing a connection with the boundary converging renormalization group, and verify its effectiveness for the case of n=2.

Research into the geometric properties of phase space for hyperbolic equations has yielded significant insights into understanding the loss of smoothness in solutions and shock formation. This method enables quantitative analysis of how certain metrics on the phase space affect the evolution of solutions over time. Building upon existing findings, our current study focuses on quasi-linear equation solutions that experience smoothness loss of the same order (less than one) as they progress temporally. By applying a change of variables, the problem is reformulated as evolution on this specific phase space. Approximating hyperbolic operators using finite Jacobi expansions allows us to develop an efficient numerical procedure for simulating solutions' behavior, even in their loss of regularity. Our new approach demonstrates, using various test functions, that the generalized phase space can extend previous results, specifically encompassing the former L2 metric as a special instance.

This research introduces several innovations in Japanese word segmentation, building upon prior endeavors. A substantial corpus compilation, comprising approximately 30 million tokenized items and accompanied by corresponding English translations, has been assembled to support this work. A recurrent neural network-based method, leveraging long-term dependencies, has been shown to boost segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, several straightforward yet effective strategies for improving segmentation precision have been devised and proposed. All of the developed resources and techniques are publicly available to facilitate open-access reproduction and advancement in Japanese word segmentation.

A notable characteristic of Stack Overflow is its extensive body of shared knowledge, particularly in the form of links to external educational resources like tutorial websites. Our study focuses on the popularity of such resources, examining the frequency with which they are used on Stack Overflow and the extent of the knowledge they convey. An analysis of the popularity of nearly 48 million SO posts, the websites they reference, and the content of the top websites, reveals several key insights. Firstly, the links to online courses and tutorial websites account for a significant proportion of the shared knowledge resources, but the knowledge provided by these sites is often dispersed across multiple SO posts, each written at a different time. Furthermore, the knowledge popularity of these sites, as measured by the number of SO posts, correlates positively with their actual popularity at web popularity, although some high-popular sites are underutilized on SO, some with a knowledge-popularity on SO.

This research explores the impact of dark matter halo substructure on galactic rotation curves, focusing on halos with isothermal cores and checking if core stability persists over long-term simulations. By integrating full 3D hydrodynamic simulations of various dwarf galaxies, our findings suggest that as long as the dark matter core remains intact, the rotation curve will remain largely unaffected by the presence of substructure, with potential fluctuations appearing only at very low velocities ($R_{core} / V_{circ} \approx 0.003$). Extending previous studies, we've demonstrated that if the galactic halo contains a central bulge or significant tidal forces, they can eliminate the dark matter core within a short simulation time. Consequently, the impact of substructure substructure on the rotation curve will inevitably emerge in such scenarios. To resolve discrepancies between $\Lambda$CDM$ $simulations and observations of some small galaxies, it has been proposed that the galactic core might collapse to form the observed uniform rotation curves and, in some cases, hexagonal or triaxial structures, in line with new observational findings on the shapes of dark matter halos.

To effectively design climate action interventions, it is essential to understand how to inspire individuals to take relevant actions against climate change. Cloudform is a system that leverages artificial intelligence to personalize these interventions by matching them to a user's unique set of values. To achieve this, Cloudform employs a sophisticated approach that involves selecting the most relevant values to consider, learning the connections between these values and climate action takeovers, and then using this knowledge to recommend the best value that aligns with each intervention. This method allows Cloudform to accurately capture the nuances of how personal values influence behavior change and cloud-native value-sensitive motivation for climate action, resulting in a substantial improvement in matching interventions to specific users' preferences.

Concurrent with the rapid expansion of online health information, there is a resulting need for more advanced systems in clinical decision support. Natural language processing has the potential to address this need by enabling external data to be integrated into the system. As an example, we are focusing on symptom extraction using text as input. This involves extracting individual symptoms from a given paragraph by labeling phrases with specific clinical terms such as "hip pain." We are aiming to enhance the extractor's ability to adapt to new domains through domain generalization by training it on multiple source domains, which in our case are distinct sets of clinical text data from various sources like Unified Medical Language System, Concept-Symptom Matrix, Clinical Text Data Mining Knowledge Base, and Electronic Health Records. By fine-tuning the trained model on a target dataset relating to concept-symptom associations, we are observing an enhancement in its association accuracy and a consequential improvement in extraction performance. Our findings indicate that utilizing domain generalization in symptom extraction yields an overall accuracy of 71%, with a 9% accuracy gain compared to training solely on the target dataset.

Our research focuses on how Reccurrent Neural Networks enhance autonomous driving capabilities, especially in situations where critical information is missing or driving conditions are extremely challenging. To capture spatial and temporal relationships in the environment, we use Long Short-Term Memory networks, which enable better exploration of hidden data and efficient modeling of multi-source sensor information. Our methodology builds on existing work and our previous studies, leveraging Multiple Recurrent States to improve prediction accuracy and target tracking in extreme situations. By integrating known and unknown environment data, our model allows the vehicle to optimize its trajectory and increase safety, ultimately allowing the vehicle to navigate more confidently and efficiently.

We suggest that Ring Neural Networks (RNNs) serve as a versatile classifier, capable of matching the performance of traditional ANN models while consuming relatively low power. By integrating memristive crossbar memory arrays, RNNs eliminate the need for additional support hardware and eliminate energy losses associated with standard memory types. Moreover, Ring Neural Networks enable the exploration of cutting-edge low-power memory technology, particularly that provided by emerging memristive arrays.

This research examines how the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter, conforming to $SU(3)_F$ symmetry, is influenced by a powerful magnetic field within the framework of relativistic quark mean field theory. By incorporating spin-orbit coupling terms that account for the interaction between quark spins and the external magnetic field, our study reveals two distinct spin alignment patterns within each flavor doublet and triplets of matter. Notably, we found that a powerful magnetic field induces a significant stiffening effect on the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter, particularly those composed of six-quark doublets. Furthermore, we discovered a unique reversal in the trend of sound speed as a function of spin alignment and magnetic field strength, which holds promise for further investigation.

The rise of internet-of-things (IoT) is transforming how individuals and businesses use personal devices, turning them into a valuable resource for contributing unused processing power to various applications. To leverage this potential, Pado enables users to synchronously share their devices' computational capabilities, significantly increasing processing power. By integrating the IOT paradigm with cloud computing's synergistic sharing concept, users can easily synchronize their devices via any social media account, secure account creation, or a QR code, making their devices available for computational task-sharing and increasing throughput by up to three times compared to using a single device. Furthermore, Pado's architecture employs a battery-aware, real-time task scheduling, dubbed Energy-aware Real-time Task Sharing (EARTS), which divides jobs into sub-tasks and schedules them across available processors without overloading any single device, also minimizing the response time's variance. In a evaluated setup with ten personal devices, Pado showed improved throughput, less response time variation, and reduced average response times compared to traditional load sharing approaches, particularly in scenarios with fluctuating workloads and power-constrained environments.

This research integrates numerical techniques for eigenvalue approximation with an efficient adaptive sampling strategy. By focusing on a collocation method for solving nonlinear eigenvalue problems, the proposed method efficiently approximates eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvfunctions using the vertices of an optimized grid. The effectiveness of this method can be attributed to the eigenfunctions and eigenvales being localized, allowing the method to be particularly effective. To validate its potential, the method was applied in a test scenario.

We explore a class of transformations known as $\beta$-transformations with intermediate stages, focusing on the measure and topology of their remainder classes mod $1/k$ where $k$ is an integer greater than $1$. Like the well-hampered properties of symbol spaces, certain intermediate sets for these $\beta$-transformations exhibit erosion, thereby allowing us to identify specific, highly complex subsets within them that retain bad approximability characteristics for non-integral bases. For degree two remainder classes, we determine the Hausdorff and packing dimensions of each, while for higher degrees up to $8$, numerical calculations provide dimensional estimates. Additionally, methods for calculating these dimensions at arbitrary precision are presented, offering potential avenues for achieving exact results.

We study $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories with $N_{F}$ fundamental quark flavors and $N_{c}=3,4,6$ employing lattice simulations. Without any gauge charge, we introduce $U(1)_{J}$ global symmetry, a $Z_{2}$ global center symmetry, multiple $U(1)$ chiral symmetries depending on $N_{F}$, and certain $U(1)_{C}$ chiral symmetry that remains unbroken due to 't Hooft anomalies. Lattice simulations reveal that pairs of quarks do not carry gauge charge due to anomaly constraints, significantly influencing the $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry breaking. We investigate whether the theories exhibit conformal fixed points or fundamental massless fermion properties by analyzing the center and chiral symmetry breaking patterns of $N_{c}=3,4,6$ with $N_{F}=8,9,10$ degenerate flavors. For $N_{c}=3,4$ with $N_{F}=8,9$, we observe center symmetry breaking and chiral symmetry breaking, indicating that these theories possess massless fermions. For $N_{c}=6$ with $N_{F}=10$, we see center symmetry breaking but the possible restoration of chiral symmetry at large source values. By having $N_{F}$ approach the conformal window, we see the $SO(N_{c})$ center

Interpreting complex X解释Y relationships in time series data poses significant challenges, especially when considering the influence of multiple external factors on Y over time. In this study, we developed an alternative approach, a novel visual interpretation, known as Disentangled Attribution Curves, which effectively accounts for temporal dynamics and temporal decoupling. This method is grounded in temporal attribution analysis of each variable's individual impact on Y and enables users to gain insight into diverse temporal patterns of effects for each variable. In our study, we demonstrate the efficacy of this disentangled attribution analysis by applying it to the task of predicting bike availability, and successfully identify key variables and temporal patterns of effects in the process.

In the field of distributed machine learning, federated learning holds significant potential, yet faces significant challenges due to potential data infringement and unreliable models. Existing privacy-preserving methods have several drawbacks: high computational and communication costs, dependence on specific assumptions, or only guaranteeing protection against particular attacks. To address these limitations, we propose a scalable and robust private federated learning approach, named FedMP, which synthesizes theoretical knowledge about attack-defence to ensure model reliability and data confidentiality. By introducing a defensive attack, we realize scale-out attack and a controllable trade-off, FedMP employs regularisation and adaptability to mitigate the impact, thus providing equitable protection for all users. We demonstrate that FedMP ensures equal protection at any network scale and protects the aggregated model against various attacks and adversarial inputs. Notably, FedMP achieves superior results compared to state-of-the-art alternatives in terms of accuracy and efficiency, requiring less computation time and offering higher accuracy at any network scale.

We've developed a groundbreaking approach to testing drivers on user-specific microcontrollers without the need for a specific type of programmer. Our solution involves three key elements: a configurable and adaptable testing environment called DriverSim, a collection of reusable drivers called DriverBank, and a series of testing procedures that involve injecting various system configurations into the testing environment. By utilizing this approach, users can populate DriverSim with real-world hardware components, initialize the drivers from DriverBank by establishing complex system configurations, and run multiple test cases on populated systems for extensive validation. DriverSim supports both Emu mode, which mimics the behavior of actual user hardware, and Rmu mode, which resets the system during each test run for enhanced isolation. DriverSim is either implemented as standalone software or can be embedded into user hardware with minimal added cost. DriverBank contains a wide range of drivers for various hardware components, enabling users to load populated systems that closely resemble their actual hardware配置. DriverSim offers a extensive set of test procedures, including the ability to verify the correct operation of individual drivers and the effective interaction between drivers.

This study introduces Timeloops, a cutting-edge solution that expedites the reverse engineering of network traffic for applications written in interpreted languages. Traditionally, this approach relies on system call tracing, which is ineffective for network activities made by interpreted languages. To overcome this limitation, Timeloops employs a combination of kernel system call tracing and application-level filtering powered by modern multi-core processors. This innovative method enables precise filter rules to be applied during runtime without compromising the original execution of the application being traced. Furthermore, Timeloops has been tested and found to produce no detectable negative impact on the performance of applications written in PHP and Python.

Single-cell RNA-seq data analysis often employs dimensionality reduction for effective data exploration and interpretation. However, analyzing high-dimensional data from 10,000 genes at a time is computationally challenging, making it difficult for both humans and machines to process. Our work introduces an innovative approach for data reduction by dividing the high-dimensional space into cells and projecting each space onto a lower-dimensional space where classification and clustering can be performed more efficiently. By considering the structure of RNA-seq data, our method develops three variants of partitioned spatial reduction: projection of cluster centers, low-rank matrix factorization, and clustering with error projection. Our findings demonstrate that product space forms outperform Euclidean spaces by as much as 10% in classification accuracy and achieved significant results with four dimensions, while accurately reconstructing the data with high fidelity, nearly 98% mean-squared-error, with no upper limit on the dimensionality of the low-dimensional spaces. We also examine the computational efficiency of our methods by comparing them to well-known algorithms such as K-means and t-SNE, as well as high-performance alternatives. Our approach is implemented in the RPKMPS package, available at http://github.com/RPKMPS/RPKMPS.

For a supermassive black hole that sits at the center of a galaxy with no surrounding halo of dark matter, we've investigated how three distinct stellar populations - uniform, mass-separated, and half uniform half halo - scatter their members around it using two approaches, a simple perturbation method and more accurate numerical simulations. We've found that to first order, perturbation calculations can give a good approximation of how energy levels change for certain types of scatterers, but this method falls short when applied to more complex mass distributions. Our findings also reveal that in all scenarios, the central cluster of stars均衡es itself on a timescale that's comparable to its shortest orbital period times a value around five.

Model Predictive Control, especially its stochastic variant, offers valuable properties for advanced motion control, yet practical implementation is hindered by high-dimensional uncertainty systems. To overcome this challenge, our method utilizes uncertainty? (rather than full probability distributions) as predictions, enabling real-time minimum distance-based uncertainty tracking within a two-stage stochastic framework. By designing an optimizer capable of handling trackable uncertainty, our approach effectively minimizes uncertainty over a prediction horizon in conjunction with current system uncertainty. This allows for efficient use of computational resources, making it suitable for execution on common platforms. The results demonstrate that our method yields comparable performance to traditional full uncertainty-based optimizers, while exceeding the performance of their deterministic counterparts in both case studies.

Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is a widely utilized technique in various compression and data analytics areas. However, its substantial memory requirements can be limiting, especially when working with large-scale datasets. To address this issue, we have developed a novel family of ICA algorithms that operate in a compressed manner, allowing them to handle high-dimensionality data with less memory. These algorithms are based on the common approach of using analytic ignition and can be implemented in two ways: one through compressive sensing and the other via inverting the mixing matrix in a limited subspace. Moreover, we provide theoretical guarantees for one variant of our algorithms by formulating it as an optimization problem with linear constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that these proposed algorithms not only save significant memory but also achieve performance close to that of conventional ICA methods, despite providing only a small number of data samples.

In an innovative theoretical framework, a voter model like the asymmetric noisy voter model is introduced on one-dimensional infinite space divided into unit-sized intervals. The model, sensitive to noise, accounts for particles exchanging positions with a certain probability within neighboring intervals. An equivalent cellular automaton version is developed, showing that in the limiting case of infinitesimal interaction radius but finite exchange probability, two competing species system behaves differently depending on parameter values - potentially leading to extinction or periodic outcomes. Additionally, an asymptotic analysis reveals the system's diffusive behavior as it evolves over time, allowing for a calculation of speed as a function of limiting parameters. Furthermore, assuming species only attempt to interact with the nearest neighbor in a directed manner, a diffusive limit is explored, revealing a non-standard behavior where speed becomes unbounded under certain diffusion coefficient growth conditions.
Building on a previous joint publication, this work expands upon it by assuming infinite extendability in the stated theorems and lemmas, with their original forms remaining valid.

A theory is developed to accurately model the spontaneous emergence of entanglement between two mechanical oscillators via a highly damped electrical circuit. The model employs a semiclassical framework that incorporates the quantum motion of the oscillators and a detailed, yet physically precise description of the circuit using classical electromagnetism. Building on this model, a first-principles approach is used to calculate entanglement properties, including entropy, Neumann entanglement, and Villain entanglement, under typically encountered weak driving conditions. The impact of parameter variations and thermal noise on entanglement is also examined, revealing that systems featuring a highly damped quantum circuit are particularly resistant to thermal noise. Furthermore, the need for active driving to maintain entanglement against decay and thermal noise while also enabling its efficient extraction is established.

A crucial component in calculating next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) real contributions in QCD is the formation of splitting operators from splitting functions. This research focuses on deriving splitting operators from specific splitting functions, including q to gg and gg to ggg, at a particular operator level, specifically at one-loop order. The calculated splitting operators are essential for creating subtraction terms that facilitate real to virtual ratio calculations, particularly in the context of real emission amplitudes within SCET II. Notably, the proposed splitting operators are consistent with real emission amplitudes up to TMD factorization.

We expand upon Greenberg's strong approximation theorem for local rings by demonstrating its viability in a broader context of rings. Specifically, we adapt the theorem to one-dimensional local rings and explore its implications beyond the original formulation. Furthermore, we investigate the theorem's applicability to certain types of domains that are not Henselian, such as two-dimensional regular domains, and draw connections to Chevalley's Cramer-Waldheim equation solution method.

This study utilized a combination of approaches, including planning, execution, analysis of data, and communication of results, in a citizen science project. The project aimed to overcome limitations in understanding sundials in Indonesia through an online platform called Instagram. By employing the公民科学 method, this research sought to address the gap in knowledge regarding sundials' historical development, usage, and spiritual significance. Through the citizen science approach, the study successfully gathered information on sundials' geographical locations, orientations, and settings, as well as performed analytical calculations. The findings showed a strong connection between the orientation of sundials and their geographical positioning, highlighting the importance of citizen science in preserving and promoting this knowledge generation process.

In a DED2D system, the general model considers a base station and multiple mobile users. The TFIET scheme selectively transmits data and energy to each user in an alternating manner. To optimize system performance, we aim to maximize the cumulative data throughput for all mobile users while adhering to multiple power supply and data transmission constraints. By formulating and breaking down the original optimization problem into two subtasks, we employ a two-stage method to resolve the issue. A conditional gradient algorithm is utilized in the first stage to determine the optimal time allocation between each user. subsequently, in the second stage, we calculate the optimal beamforming vectors using a conditional gradient algorithm. Furthermore, we investigate how to reduce computational complexity in certain special cases. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme efficiently balances data and energy transfer, leading to significant improvements in overall system performance and throughput optimality.

The rise in automation of experimental projects has been particularly noticeable due to the heightened demand for remote work arrangements, as illustrated by the experiences gained from over a decade of automated near-threshold photonics measurements. The specific application, involving precise length measurements using interferometry, has been solved through a combination of automated positioning, laser alignment, and error reduction techniques, all achieved via software-based methods. The implementation of these strategies has resulted in a substantial decrease in setup time, with a more consistent outcome, by minimizing operator-dependent variability.

We explore the connection between P and NP through the lens of rational non-integer eigenvalues of finite, undirected bipartite graphs, building upon previous work by Alon et al., which used all finite graphs. Our key contribution is a demonstration that restricting graph type to undirected bipartite graphs still fulfills Asser's conjecture, implying that P is a subset of the class $\mathcal{Spec}$. This finding necessitates developing a more complex algorithm, as previously established by Enyemfami and the author, and allows us to expand on ideas first proposed by Jenkins and the author, as detailed in a separate publication. By spuriously splitting into directed and undirected components, we can reduce the problem for directed bipartite graphs to a polynomial-time computation of its spectrum, thereby resolving instances where restricting graph type impacts P vs NP.

For the purpose of building electrostatic phase plates, we've developed a novel design approach based on the multi-gate field effect transistor, which allows for flexible adjustment of their structural parameters such as the density and distribution of gates. The critical dimensions of our devices were kept within 500 nm using standard lithography techniques. Following fabrication, the number and spatial arrangement of gates were verified using various microscopy methods. According to our simulations, the number of gates significantly affects the number of transmitted electrons, the size of the electron probe and the distribution of electrons over the gate array. The number of gates with multiple orientations also impacts the probe size. The findings were validated by comparing them with experimental results.

We introduce a unified theoretical framework that encompasses physical computation, quantum computation, and one potential future advancement, all based on a singular mechanism: extraction of computed information through collision processes between charged particles. This unified approach emphasizes computation as an energy-transfer enabled information-extraction process, a perspective distinct from traditional computational models. The framework's validity is substantiated by a thorough comparison with existing models, highlighting its potential to energy-efficiently compute through charged-particle interaction, which could offer a more efficient alternative to current methods while also shedding light on the interconnection between quantum computation and future advancements.

For individuals living in a hypercube of size $n$ within a $d$-dimensional space, the count of a specific individual's visits to a designated person's location follows a Poisson distribution with a mean of $\mu = \frac{2d}{\pi} \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2d+1}\right)$. We establish both a lower and an upper bound for this visit count, observing its asymptotic behavior as $\mu = O(d)$. We derive a normal approximation for the count excess, demonstrating an asymptotic normality coefficient of $\asymp 1/\sqrt{d}$. Our findings indicate that hypercubes in different dimensions Poisson-distribute visits, while tori in different dimensions normally distribute these visits.

This study explores the quantum correction to the Schwarzschild metric, which is derived by applying the Schr\"{o}dinger equation to a particle moving in a curved spacetime. As this correction increases, the Schwarzschild black hole (SBH) transforms into a polymer black hole (PBH). By examining the backreaction effect, which is calculated using the Newman-Unti-Tamburino-Wheeler (NUTW) and Kodama vectors, it becomes apparent that the SBH's singularity is replaced by an ultralight compact object featuring an event horizon and a smooth, circular naked singularity. In the kinetic term, the PBHS exhibits a wormhole-like structure due to the emergence of an Einstein rod. By applying the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkov equation, which is used to describe the equilibrium of a fluid of neutrons, we demonstrate that the PBHS transforms into a ultralight compact object without an event horizon when the kinetic energy is dominated, which is consistent with our previous findings using the Newtonian approximation. In the non-relativistic regime, a similar result is obtained. By utilizing a photometric analysis of the light ring in the shadow of black holes, which can be observed through radial photons, we find that the PBHS transforms into a ultralight compact object when the kinetic term is significantly greater than the mass, which is consistent with our findings using the Newtonian approximation.

In a theoretical framework for modeling doped graphene, we investigated how its physical properties change when subjected to quantum fluctuations using the random phase approximation. Our analysis focused on the impact of quasiparticle velocity and Fermi velocity on the system's behavior, particularly in relation to dimensionality. We calculated the ratio of heat capacity to temperature for different spatial dimensions. Our results show that velocity reduction amplifies heat capacity, allowing the system to be physically interpreted in terms of an effectively lower doping level. These findings are compared to experimental data, and we observe that by increasing the quasiparticle velocity, the system's heat capacity can be made to align with measurements.

In this report, we introduce a novel neural masked speech transformation approach called MaskedSpeech that generates highly natural and expressive speech with minimal training data. Unlike traditional training methods that involve extensive datasets, MaskedSpeech can be effectively trained using only a few hours of labeled data by combining a self-attention based encoder and a 1D convolutional decoder. To improve the system's performance, we designed an innovative masking strategy allowing the model to process entire character-level sequences, thereby demonstrating superior speech synthesis quality compared to the previous state-of-the-art method, NCS.

High-dimensional Bayesian Gaussian Graphical Models (BGGM) aim to reconstruct the genetic interaction network by estimating the precision matrix of a multivariate Gaussian distribution based on genetic expression data of large dimension. Due to the extensive number of potential model combinations, classical approaches typically employ approximation techniques combined with regularization to select relevant variables and promote model approximation. Conversely, our proposal stems from a fully conjugate variational inference framework that evolves mean-field variational inference. By leveraging this method, we can precisely retain each gene's selected subset and its associated posterior uncertainty derived from the original model, without compromise. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, yielding superior results compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.

This paper's first contributor tackles multiple countermeasures against deep learning network vulnerabilities, encompassing In-the-Middle attacks and adversarial examples. A distinct feature of Man-in-the-Middle attacks is their ability to manipulate data in real-time, unlike pre-trained adversarial examples. Our approach involves deploying multiple attack strategies aimed at forcing a DNN misclassification of incoming data while capturing real-time traffic. While adversarial examples often rely on optimization techniques, our method utilizes simple arithmetic operations to maximize their
impact. As a result, we've discovered that even basic attacks can accomplish our objectives under a Man-in-the-Middle scenario. Additionally, we've discovered that techniques used to mitigate adversarial examples can also provide protection against Manipulation under a Man-in-the-Middle scenario. Through experiments on various classification models, we've verified the feasibility of our strategies on the ImageNet dataset, even in the presence of sophisticated attacks.

Recent research has established a link between climate change denial online and conspiracy theories. Our study examines the content strategies used by conspiracy theory websites to discuss climate change, focusing on climate change denial as a prominent theme. By analyzing manually collected website content, we discovered that climate change deniers are among the most active deniers, frequently appearing in articles and videos. Unlike other deniers, they are not consistently promoted across website platforms. Despite this, some websites make no references to the global climate crisis at all. Our results indicate that conspiracy theory websites rely on climate change denial to engage readers, but it is not their primary focus, and they use similar tactics to introduce credible scientific terminology to validate their claims.

Spent Fuel Assemblies were utilized as highly sensitive detectors within the Experiment with Real Assets in INFN's Laboratori del Gran Sasso experiment.
