Expanding upon this research, we investigate additional notable operators - the超几何函数 operator and the Lamé operator - to demonstrate that their eigenvalue problems also exhibit connections to well-known special functions in quantum physics and mathematical physics, namely hypergeometric functions and Jacobi functions, respectively. Likewise, the eigenvectors associated with these operators exhibit similarities to the Dirac operator's eigenvectors and can be interpreted as resulting from further special integrations.

In this study, we compare the average communication capabilities of vehicles in two types of networks - one with relays and no relays - using accurate mathematical models. We consider a complex vehicle network where vehicles move randomly and use base stations to transmit data, along with some relays that can forward data to vehicles. Our analysis shows that even though the number of relays increases, the overall communication efficiency of vehicles using relays isn't always significantly better than without relays, under certain base station load conditions. However, the non-linearity of signal reception via relays does contribute to more diverse patterns of communication opportunities among vehicles.

Our main goal in this study is to enhance the quality of automatic sentence labeling on Wikipedia articles in machine-readable formats. To achieve this, we focus on high-traffic, manually updated sections of each article where we utilize edit history to identify low-quality sentences that can be poorly constructed, incoherent, or irrelevants. By utilizing a machine-learning approach we utilize labeling behaviors of experienced and novice editors to create accurate labels for these difficult sentences, we show that these weaker models can generate high-quality labels that serve as effective training data, we utilize specialized linguistic and Wikipedian features to supplement editing patterns, we analyze and visualize the labeling decisions made by editors to understand and leverage these insights.

A versatile teaching technique known as black-box knowledge distillation (B3) generates a smaller model with a different framework that mimics the predictions of a larger model with several times its size. Traditional B3 methods rely on access to the training data, which is not the case with our decision-based B3 (DB3) approach. Unlike other B3 methods that employ image reconstruction, our DB3 method is purely decision-driven and uses reinforcement learning to create a compact model with excellent performance. The results show that our architecture outperforms current B3 approaches by achieving exceptional accuracy on imageNet, producing images with impressive quality on ImageNet-Challenge, and excelling in medical image classification on two imageNet subsets and 2D/3D CT scans out ofperforming the leading model, Clip.100 with only using 100 images.

Using data collected between 2009 and 2018 with the LHCb detector, a significant uncertainty of 1% is estimated for the average number of electrons produced in the decay of the B-sigma-plus particle, in addition to two neutrons. This estimate includes technical and statistical errors, as well as an uncertainty of 0.0078 in the sum of two integers that determine the measurement's sensitivity, arising from the detector's performance. This measurement is based on the comparison of the signal events, in which the b-quark decays into the sigma-plus particle, with sidebands, in which a charm-quark decays into the same particle. The relevant decay modes are as follows: sigma-plus particle plus two neutrons plus a positron plus a muon (signal) and sigma-plus particle plus two neutrons plus a proton plus two muons (sidebands). The results have been published with the following references: LHCb detector (2008), LHCb information and regularities (2013), and the LHCb collaboration's latest findings on the efficiency of the detector in 2018, as well as the efficiency of the detector in 2018, as well as the efficiency of the detector in 2018, as well as the efficiency of the detector in 2018, as well as the efficiency of the detector in 2018,

String theory's homogeneous spaces can be represented by specific trivial extensions of Lie groups in certain contexts. We investigate the connection between the classical T-duality's action on geometric T-duals and the mechanical involution in these scenarios. The broader implication of our analysis is that continuous-trace algebras over group manifolds potentially possess multiple classical T-duals, with at least one of them being a twisted classical T-dual. Our findings reinforce the notion that the classification of continuous-trace algebras through projections and Hilbert $C^*$-bimodules is aligned with T-duality's principles.

Current imitation learning techniques typically depend on learning from example actions provided by experts, but this comes with the drawbacks of requiring experts to demonstrate every possible action and maintaining consistency in the way they perform those actions. By leveraging the correlations between different tasks, the limitations of these methods can be overcome even when the tasks are only slightly related. Moreover, this approach not only enhances imitation learning but also leads to the generation of effective skills that can be applied across a range of tasks and even applied to behavior understanding. The technique allows agents to figure out latent behavior variables that drive actions by observing how changes in these variables affect the agent's behavior in the context of multiple tasks. As a result, the agent can figure out the underlying relationship between input and output variables across diverse tasks without ever seeing those outputs directly, leading to outstanding performance on various benchmark tasks, including those involving variable manipulation, object use, and the use of tools.

We derive an asymptotic expression for the error probability of a sequential decoder with polar bias, under the assumption of time-varying binary symmetric channels. We show that using a polarized cutoff rate as the bias yields a lower error probability than previously demonstrated, particularly when the cutoff is estimated from the current codeword portion and only applicable to sequential decoders with fixed bias. A new, effective variance estimation for the log-likelihood ratio (LLR) list codeword estimator is also developed, which is crucial in obtaining the stated error probability asymptotics.

This research introduces a computer vision technique to monitor hands and objects in their natural movements. By training a unique model on a single image, it's able to capture the complex dynamics of hand-object interactions, such as occlusions and rotations. The tracking system is built on a recurrent structure that integrates a 3D convolutional model and a visible-surface tracking mechanism. By leveraging past frames, our method successfully tracks objects behind the hand and navigates through all these challenges. The proposed system demonstrates its ability to capture fine-grained details and automate the process of tracking hands and objects across various scenarios, with minimal training requirements.

In the realm of finite field reduced groups of extraspecial type, we classify and identify only $2$-groups, ultimately demonstrating that it is possible for a reduced extraspecial $2$-group to exist. Furthermore, we show through examples that it is impossible for groups of order $pq$ and $p^2q$ to be reduced.

A conventional method for establishing a robot's external frame of reference involves using a calibration tool called a fiducial, which typically consists of a series of markers arranged in a predetermined 3D shape. Traditional estimation methods mainly rely on a robot's camera system, which can only observe the fiducial's two-dimensional representation and calculate its pose. However, this method is quite sensitive to noise and can be easily disrupted by obstacles. In this research, we take advantage of an end-effector equipped with a depth sensor to enhance the external estimation process. By combining the depth information with the robot's camera system, we can accurately determine the markers' positions and improve pose estimation performance. Furthermore, we propose a novel estimation technique, which treats the markers as random variables and applies an optimal estimation method to generate reliable results with defined uncertainty levels. The effectiveness of this depth-assisted external estimation method is validated through a thorough analysis.

Researchers often face a significant challenge when conducting field and lab experiments, which is identifying whether treatment given to one subject affects the outcomes of other subjects within the same group. Successfully answering this question hinges on correctly identifying the unit where potential interference through a treatment may occur. While many studies make clear assumptions about where potential interference may lie, many others fail to do so and instead consider the entire network as affected. In this study, we develop an elegant statistical test to detect interference, which is robust to differences in network structure, network size and network density. The key innovation of this test is that it does not need to explicitly determine the unit where potential interference may lie, which was previously thought to be essential. Instead, we show that network variability can be harnessed to isolate the impact of treatment on subjects, without explicitly identifying the focal unit where potential interference may lie. Through two case studies, we illustrate the importance of selecting the appropriate focal unit for isolation and network sampling strategies that can increase power to detect interference. The ability to identify interference, even when network structure is unknown and heterogeneous, provides a valuable tool for researchers.

The formation and thermal evolution of neutron stars and white dwarfs can be accelerated by dark matter self-annihilation within the stars. This acceleration accelerates cooling in neutron stars and causes premature contraction in white dwarfs. By analyzing a white dwarf's rapid contraction and cooling, researchers establish an upper limit on the dark matter annihilation cross-section, which must be below 0.55 pb in a specific mass range, 50-700 MeV/c^2.

Our investigation focuses on the performance of ShapePipe, a multi-threaded pipeline for measuring galaxy shapes, as it would be relevant for large-scale cosmological weak-lensing studies using optical telescopes. In conjunction with other significant findings, we report that ShapePipe displays high levels of accuracy and speed, effectively multi-processing at levels up to 100 times the levels of legacy measurements, while maintaining the reliability and precision necessary for extensive optical surveys. We also found that thread synchronization challenges can have a minimal impact on the overall output, largely survey-dependent, and can be minimized through strategic model selection in certain cases. Additionally, our analysis has established that the output from ShapePipe is consistent across different survey setups through the use of standardized galaxy potential models. We have integrated ShapePipe into the public version of pyromoph, a widely-used galaxy morphology code, for the purposes of further development and future applications of large-scale optical surveys.

We resolve Veech's discrete 2-circle problem by connecting it to a property of geodesic flow on a modified version of the underlying surface. This modifies the original problem into equivalent questions about period sets of certain Hamiltonian flows. By analyzing the geometry of these flow periods, we can interpret Veech's conjecture in terms of the commutativity of specific numerical sets. Further investigation into these Hamiltonian flows allows us to prove Veech's conjecture for a broad category of geodesic flows with three frequencies, encompassing nearly all cases where the underlying surface has a finite mapping class group.

We establish a new method for determining k-rationality in hypersurfaces, improving upon previous adaptations of the Noether-Lefschetz theorem. Our finding proves that a hypersurface is k-rational if and only if its structure can be described using an exponent that does not exceed its dimension, thereby characterizing k-rationality through this minimal exponent. This insight leads to a novel criterion for identifying non-k-rational hypersurfaces, which in turn facilitates the discovery of primary examples of non-k-trivial divisors on k-rational threefolds, offering potentially infinite variations.

We examine how a magnetic field influences spin interactions in the material [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2] (D1222p), which exhibits spin-1/2 alpha-ruler geometry with strong ferromagnetic alpha interactions. D1222p displays significant spin fluctuations that can be quantitatively measured down to very low temperatures of 1.5 K. In contrast to similar materials, which typically undergo quantum phase transitions at high magnetic fields, D1222p's spin fluctuations remain consistent with the field. We developed a spin model that incorporates the experiment's outcomes by incorporating the magnetic field's effect on the material's spin energy levels. Our findings for the material's short-range spin behavior match theoretical predictions from the spin-only model with remarkable precision, which underlines the model's effectiveness in describing D1222p's magnetic properties. Our study highlights the role of field-induced spin excitations at finite temperatures and provides a framework for understanding the material's spin behavior.

Assuming the Early Universe Strongly Interacting (a'uMSM) model's five-dimensional structure, where the model features the product of an additional universe and a circle, we investigate its capability in resolving both the strong CP issue and the instability of the electroweak vacuum through radiative corrections. Featuring five-dimensional Higgs and gluon fields, the a'uMSM model includes a four-dimensional complex axion, the U(1)_{em} gauge field, and massive Kaluza-Klein KK modes of the W and B gauge fields to tackle the strong CP problem via radiative mechanisms. Additionally, the model introduces nontrivial radiative corrections to the Higgs potential that stabilize the electroweak vacuum. Furthermore, the theory predicts novel interactions between the KK modes and particles at the LHC, which could be experimentally verified through distinctive signatures such as resonant production of pairs of photons, leptons, or bosons.

Quantic Technology is generating significant interest due to its vast computational capabilities, which surpass those of classical computers. Currently, researchers are exploring the underlying principles of quantum mechanics to solve complex, intractable problems in chemistry, physics, and other fields of study. However, quantum systems are extremely difficult to replicate classically when all the Clifford and T gates are involved in quantum circuit compositions. Consequently, quantum computers are not outperforming classical systems, especially when dealing with large-scale algorithms, such as the Shor algorithm. This study presents an innovative, probabilistic approach to quantum circuit simulation that utilizes a hybrid of arithmetic operations in the ring $\mathbb{Z}_r$ to improve classical computing performance. By applying prime factorization, any quantum circuit made up of Clifford and T gates can be computationally classified and calculated based on its prime components to calculate the resulting probability outputs. This approach leads to two primary outcomes: (1) identifying the quantum circuit's classical complexity for the purpose of approximating probability outputs, and (2) analyzing the influence of individual gates on circuit complexity to guide future quantum algorithm design. By integrating prime-based calculations with existing classical algorithms, our proposed method enables the efficient, high-precision classification of quantum circuit complexity for future applications in chemistry, physics, cryptography, and other areas of study.

We conducted a comprehensive binary catalog creation based on the LAMOST time-domain survey by analyzing the drift-scan data from 2020 and scheduled observations on a total of 11 specific targets for lacturnae, variable stars, and binary stars, which were recorded between 2020 and 2021. Using the analysis of spatial distribution and orbital movement of lacturnaries, we defined the binary candidates effectively. We designed an initial selection process to filter out lacturnaries, and then applied two machine learning methods, including a random forest classifier and logistic regression, to further refines the binary candidates. This approach resulted in a catalog containing 3,745,969 binary candidates and 1,544 confirmed binary stars within our target range. This catalog is publicly accessible at the link https://astroml.org/lamost/lamost-bc/.

The focus of this work is on developing a true random number generator (TRNG) specifically optimized for use in AI/ML inference on edge computing devices. In aid of this goal, a new 26-transistor TRNG, known as TuRaN TRNG, was designed, which utilizes the threshold shifts of a 6-T inverter chain triggered by a start signal to create large analog variations serving as a seeding input for digital noise generation. By integrating the 6-T inverter chain within the start signal cell, the need for external storage of the random state is eliminated, allowing the newly generated random numbers to be produced continuously in a pipelined fashion. Utilizing different extraction techniques and a post-processing method known as von Neumann extraction, two versions of the TuRaN TRNG were realized and demonstrated to achieve throughput rates 10 to 100 times higher, along with energy consumption levels orders of magnitude lower, compared to conventional TRNGs. Through rigorous testing using industry standard tools as well as in-depth analysis across a range of process, voltage, and temperature conditions, it was verified that the TuRaN TRNG successfully produces high-quality random numbers by passing all industry standard tests under varying operating conditions. Notably, the TuRaN TRNG was shown capable of generating one random bit per transistor switching event, and as such, it was projected to outperform existing TRNG technologies by factors as high as 10,000 in terms

A unique on-off current feature of a resistance change device that operates on single-electron principles has been demonstrated through experiments. This device is composed of an Al oxide and Au nanowire structure. The switch exhibits a significant on/off current ratio of around 10^-3, which is much lower than typical resistive memory technology. However, it offers several advantages such as a supply voltage as low as 25 mV, a switching current that can be adjusted without a read-out voltage, and a write/erase mechanism based on a simple voltage reversal.

We apply causal representation to Feynman integrands in complex multi-loop calculations, and its utility has been proven through the successful calculation of compactly supported scattering forms at two loops and the reduction of Feynman integrals in double box examples.

This study examines the connection between the spectral measures and the Green functions of quantum walks, both within the discrete torus $\Tori$ and the infinite lattice $\Zdi^d$. By leveraging the properties of the Green functions for quantum walks, we can both bound the spectral measures and gain insight into the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Laplacian on these spaces. To achieve this, we first analyze the Green functions on the infinite lattice $\Zdi^d$ using asymptotic expansions and the Fourier series, then extend this investigation to the discrete torus $\Tori$ by exploiting the relationship between the Green functions of the two spaces, leading to an expression of the Green function on the torus as a sum of the infinite lattice Green function and an asymptotic expansion.

By merging two distinct models of quark matter behavior under high pressure, we have developed two star models to better understand the inner workings of hybrid stars. We have also used two distinct models to describe the pressure-dependent behavior of their surrounding surroundings. With these combinations, we have examined the complete profiles of four neuon stars that closely resemble Kepler's XJTUJ1853-10. We have also examined how mass and radius are affected differently by these unique internal and external compositions and have determined the optimal surface shapes along with their accompanying tidal deformations. We have also calculated the temperature profiles within these neuon stars using the most current data available. We have found that when considering only one model of quark matter behavior, there is no phase transition within the star's core, whereas incorporating two models results in two distinct states within the star separated by the point of quark transformation, resulting in more pronounced changes in radius and tidal deformability. We have found that increasing the point of quark transformation within the star results in increased radius and tidal deformability values and decreased mass values. We have found that combining two models of quark matter behavior results in increased tidal deformability values compared to bosonic models under the same conditions.

In this study, we investigate an optomechanical system which combines a nonlinear $q$-deformed beam splitter with a single cavity mode that interacts with an optomechanical oscillator through both optomechanical coupling and tunneling effects. Our analysis focuses on how these interactions influence the behavior of the optomechanical oscillator in terms of steady states and fluctuating averages. Furthermore, we examine steady-state correlations and employ the linear response theory to evaluate the output statistics of the probe field as a function of optomechanical tunneling strength and $q$-deformation parameter. Our demonstrated results indicate that by adjusting these parameters, one can effectively manipulate the steady-state behavior of the optomechanical oscillator and achieve significant enhancements in the statistically fluctuating output probe field transmission coefficient. Our investigation provides a foundational understanding that could facilitate the development of high-performance sensing mechanisms for detecting weak signals.

This study creates a detailed comparison between the transition probabilities for electric dipole transitions in isovector and inverse isovector modes, specifically at the 1ph state, in two similar atomic nuclei: $^{120}$Sn and $^{116}$Mo. Using the Random Phase Approximation, we calculated ph and 2p2h transition strengths with a focus on v-interactions based on the modified Skyrme Hartree-Fock energy density functional. Our analysis revealed that in both studied nuclei, the negative modes exhibit significantly stronger transitions than the positive ones, with a ratio of approximately 0.2. This differs from the commonly observed behavior in R-positive scissors modes, where inverting the direction of the transition increases strength by at most a factor of two. Additionally, our findings indicate that electric dipole transitions in R-negative modes primarily target protons, whereas R-positive transitions can be equally influenced by neutrons and protons depending on the configuration. These results are consistent with previously conducted experiments that have identified R-negative states in the vicinity of stable nuclei such as $^{116}$Sn, $^{124}$Xe, and $^{166}$Yb, and suggest that they may appear as states with unusual magnetic properties in magnetic resonance studies.

This investigation examines the phenomenon of unsually pronounced metal-to-insulator transition observed in graphene, driven by its electronic confinement effects at extremely low dimensions. Employing the approach of quasiparticle unscreened Coulomb energy with the image charge effect considered to describe the unscreened long-range Coulomb interaction in plane-like systems, we calculate the critical dimension characterizing the transition through analysis of the quasiparticle energy spectrum. Using the framework of Landau parameters within the framework of quasiparticle interaction in Fermi liquids we compute the unscreened Coulomb energy with the image charge effect considered and obtain the critical dimension without making additional assumptions. Also, its dependence on the quasiparticle interaction parameter is examined.

Our work merges established statistical principles with cutting-edge research on laser-cooled atomic groups. By applying analytical methods to well-documented theories, we show that, as is typical with random events, their occurrence frequencies adhere to a predictable pattern characterized by significant uncertainty at lower probabilities. Furthermore, due to the unique properties of these atoms, we observe a distinct decrease in uncertainty at lower probabilities. To test these theoretical findings, we collaborate with partners to run a series of experiments, initially confirming the predicted patterns through basic visual inspection of the data.

In March 2021, an analysis of the global cryptocurrency trading network was conducted, following an unprecedented surge in the cryptocurrency market's volume. After analyzing 11 major currencies represented by their trade tokens, numerous striking patterns were uncovered, particularly when examining both direct and indirect connections between these currencies. As if performing a delicate dance, these currencies interacted with each other, often shifting from intricate interactions to more straightforward exchanges. Specifically, the market experienced a significant increase in transaction volumes during March through August, 2021, thereby increasing the market's complexity, only to witness a sudden shift in dynamics during late August when major announcements were made. During this surge, one currency, representing a specific major currency, formed connections with ten others, while simultaneously forging new, potentially more stable relationships with the remaining currencies. A closer look at these connections reveals a intriguing phenomenon where some relationships appear to be indirectly influenced by a specific major currency, even in cases where a direct connection does not exist.

A combined approach of ab-initio calculations and path integral methods applied to the association of H2SO4 and (H2O)1-3 clusters sheds light on the impact of zero-point energy on proton transfer within the interaction of sulphuric acid and water. Our findings suggest that dynamic effects significantly facilitate proton transfer, notably within the pentacoordinated TS2 transition state. This is characterized by a narrow potential energy surface and high ZPE, resulting in a substantial PE surface fluctuation. Furthermore, we observe a reversal in structural motifs from covalent to hydrogen-bonded as a consequence of dynamic effects.

Consider a uniformly continuous group action of G on a metric space X and its associated space of equivariant non-expansive operators from X to itself, denoted as Maps_E^d(X,X). It is shown that under specific conditions, the space of such operators can be isometrically embedded within a compact space. The research also investigates the relationship between the compactness of Maps_E^d(X,X) and the total boundedness of the metric space X, establishing that they are directly connected. Furthermore, the study examines these considerations in the context of semi-simple Lie groups, identifying total boundedness with the compactness of such group actions.

This study examines molecular transport across a membrane at a non-uniform temperature to investigate machine learning's capabilities in modeling biochemical processes. We conduct a detailed numerical analysis, machine learning model, and discuss the limitations of the Einstein relation and Fick's first law in scenarios with varying temperature profiles. The model's performance improves with the use of the thermal gradient, defined as the product of the diffusion coefficient and mobility. We compare its outcomes with another approach that models membrane transport based on the local equilibrium assumption.

Recent model comparisons in deep learning have utilized data-dependent measures of model complexity, like the spectral norm, to utilize training techniques such as parameter regularizations that promote simpler models with enhanced generalization. Nevertheless, these techniques are largely applied in a heuristic manner despite being extensively studied. We conducted a systematic study on the impact of three dominant training heuristics on model complexity and found that while the expected value of the spectral norm is influenced by the regularization of cross-entropy entropy and linear losses and data-mixup, the parameter noise used to trim model size is ineffective. We provide additional insights into the interplay between these interactions and the balancing of loss functions with improved understanding of their weighted combinations. We also discovered an unexpected effect of regularization and mixup on the higher-order properties of the spectral norm, which can result in misleading generalization estimates. To address this, we introduced an experimental method using the Jensen-Shannon divergence to approximate the cross-entropy's non-linear regularization contribution to model complexity. To complement this, we perform an iterative search for an adjusted mixup ratio that counteracts bias and accelerate the rate of growth of the spectral norm, which is then utilized to perform genuine generalization comparisons without the influence of artificial generalization boost.

This study utilizes an advanced unbinned maximum likelihood fit to analyze the decay processes of the $B^0_s \to J/\psi\pi^0$ and $B^0_s \to J/\psi\pi^+$ reactions using data collected from $101.3$ pb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collisions. By applying this method, we identify $3216$ $B^0_s$ responses associated with reactions that involve $\pi^0$ decay and $657$ $B^0_s$ responses associated with $\pi^0$ decay reactions. Through fits to the measured mass distributions in these reactions, we determine the relative branching fraction ratio $\frac{\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to \pi^0)}{\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to \pi^+)\mathcal{B}(\pi^+ \to \mu^+ \mu^-)}$ to $3.1 \times 10^{-4}$ with a statistical uncertainty of $1.1 \times 10^{-4}$ and a chirality change suppression factor of $-1.77 \pm 0.16 \pm 0.02 \pm 0.02$. With the help of an unbinned maximum likelihood fit, we also enhance our determination of the $B^0_s$ decay constant by $15\%$. The fit plays

The availability of limited quality reference data has posed a significant challenge in developing automated essay grading systems. In this study, we investigated whether training data augmentation can overcome this problem. We created a comprehensive framework for augmenting student essays based on linguistic knowledge and statistical analysis, allowing us to expand the available data by a factor of up to 50x. We evaluated our method using two leading automatic scoring models with both enlarged and original datasets. We found that while our augmented data resulted in slight improvements in some aspects of model performance, such as score prediction accuracy and style preservation, there were concerns with its ability to generalize to new writing styles and potential reduction in writing complexity.

We investigate methods for determining key parameters in models that enforce marginal independence constraints, covering notable cases such as hidden Markov models and HMMs with concealed Markov processes. Focusing on discrete states and observations, our analysis centers on two techniques: direct EM algorithms and digEST techniques, the latter utilizing optimization in the difference image space to establish the theoretical basis of the methods and provide clear insights into their computations.

The distribution of opportunities within a community has profound implications for its long-term societal structure, particularly as opportunities influence the social and economic standing of subsequent generations. To address this concern, our model incorporates a system where opportunities are not guaranteed but rather uncertain, and are passed down from one individual to another in an intergenerational framework. Since the community's rules are designed to be equitable, any opportunity one individual acquires through this system should, on average, yield the same outcome as any other individual's opportunity. Through this model, the first generation's outcomes can be represented as a combination of two distinct elements: an allocation common to all individuals (pooling effect) and individual-specific random variables (idiosyncratic effects). To determine the allocation that minimizes inequality within the community, our model employs a model-independent approach, utilizing the optimal transport theory to identify a balance between efficiency and equality in resource distribution. To achieve this, the allocation is determined by minimizing the transport cost from the idosyncratic effects to the total outcomes, measured by a strictly convex cost function. To further understand the relationship between these variables, our model seeks to identify conditions under which the convex cost function can be represented as the sum of the two distinct elements, thereby facilitating insight into the effects of opportunity allocation on social and economic structure.

In this study, the concept of particle permutation and its impact on a system's total wavefunction is critically examined, keeping in mind the requirements set by quantum mechanics for elementary particle behavior. The examples focus on two fermions and two bosons, taking particle spin into account as per the permutation-parity relationship for their wavefunctions.

The Rising Cryptos company is developing an innovative adaptation of RingCT by employing dual key signatures, a breakthrough that significantly improves transaction speed and facilitates multi-hop mixing. Our approach yields on-chain key aggregation, leading to enhanced scalability. The resulting off-mixer state can be efficiently verified, significantly accelerating mixing times. Furthermore, we have designed a straightforward protocol for coordinators to manage mixing processes and an off-mixer entry protocol that allows participants to select optimal input-output pairs, thus preserving user privacy.

This brief follows up on our previous research about approximately solving systems of linear equations within the complexity class PPT. We examine how to categorize these approximate solutions based on the reduction types used - specifically polynomial-time quantum and probabilistic classical reductions. We develop frameworks for these reductions that can be represented by quantum and classical circuits.

Our main findings include:
1. An efficient quantum circuit can be designed to solve an approximate system of linear equations if an efficient quantum circuit can solve another similar system.
2. Certain approximate linear systems are universally solvable by any other system within a constant factor. To demonstrate this, we create specific examples of such systems and prove their efficiency. These new examples are constructed from fundamental problems in number theory, highlighting the significance of quantum and classical reductions in this context.

Researchers have compiled a combined dataset for the measurement of the rare and frequent gauge boson processes WWW and WWZ using data gathered from proton-proton collisions at the 7 and 8 TeV energy levels, analyzed by the CMS experiment at CERN. The findings for the individual performance of the WWW and WWZ processes are reported as deviations from predicted standards model expectations, at 2.4 and 2.1 sigma levels respectively. Additionally, the research contains a detailed comparison between the observed data and the predictions made by the standard model for both processes.

The last two decades have seen significant growth in the field of Arabic-script Hebrew NLP, primarily driven by the widespread use of UD treebanks. This growth, however, was hindered by a lack of high-quality Hebrew training data. Our study overcomes this limitation by analyzing a newly created UD Hebrew treebank and utilizing novel approaches to train a state-of-the-art Hebrew NLP model using a data-driven strategy that bypasses the dependence on training data. Our model showcases remarkable resilience to data scarcity by achieving a 10 point increase in accuracy when trained on 10x less data, thereby setting a new benchmark for the community.

J. Bourgain demonstrated in 1989 that any epsilon-isometry of dimension n can be reduced to a combination of an epsilon-isometry and an epsilon-vector in infinite-dimensional space ell_infinity. We show that this epsilon-isometry can be chosen to have a norm of at most 1+O epsilon (n^-1/2), proving that the unit ball of ell_infinity allows for epsilon-isometric dimension reduction via linear operators only when epsilon is 1 or infinity. Additionally, excluding dimension reductions to both ell_1 and ell_infinity, we establish that dimension reductions to any other ell_p space (p not in {1,2,infinity}) are also impossible for the unit ball of ell_p when p is not equal to 2.

In continuum mechanics, plasticity models are used to describe a wide range of phenomena, but modeling history-dependent behavior like the Prager model of elasticity-plasticity requires proceeding, which is inefficient and costly. Our approach proposes a more efficient method by using a modified problem formulation that enables continuous learning, allowing us to capture the prager model's behavior without retraining from scratch. Using a U-net architecture to make a predictive model, we demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations with various loading conditions, showing that the method can accurately model the prager model and even allow for prediction under entirely new loading conditions.

Low-Density Parity-Check compact system, a subset of polar codes, leverages LDPC codes by subjecting them to various permutations, rotations, and puncturing. Based on our previous findings, a permutation approach maximizes the benefits of the subset, thus improving the maximum tolerable erasure probability of the code. Using LDPC matrices with decreasing degree correlation, particularly those with negative degree correlation, yields substantial improvements, which aligns with existing research. However, generating such matrices efficiently remains challenging. Our study proposes a novel, linear-time, greedy algorithm to generate negative degree correlation LDPC matrices in linear scale, which enables rapid generation. Our simulation results demonstrate a maximum tolerable erasure probability enhancement of over 10% with the proposed algorithm, thus facilitating the creation of permuted system compact signals more swiftly.

This note proposes the Multi-Agent Pre-and-Post-Scaled Feedback (MPSF) scheme as a method to guarantee pre- and post-scale safety and reachability for linear systems under bounded disturbances. By designing control laws in a scaled coordinates framework, we can successfully synthesize control laws that ensure safety and reachability, which would otherwise be unachievable due to unavoidable disturbances. The MPSF scheme finds a subset of control parameters that meet necessary linear inequalities, which can be efficiently computed using the algorithm introduced in our previous work. By extending the MPSF scheme, we show that it remains robust to communication delays and absence of knowledge about system parameters, making it a valuable tool for communication-constrained networks.

Our proposed attack on quantum key distribution uses a vacuum+weak decoy state approach, exploiting the eavesdropper's ability to go undetected due to the absence of a photon leakage opportunity in this method. In contrast to other systems, our attack on the vacuum+weak decoy state QKD does not cause detectable differences in error rates when the eavesdropper's activity is active, which leaves it harder to uncover. In order to calculate the unconditionally secure key rate, we take into account the possible influence of a man-the-middle attack, as well as channel loss. By comparing our calculated key rate on fiber channels, we find that the extent to which our attack reduces its effectiveness is more significant than in other attacks using the same principle. In addition, our results show that the vacuum+weak decoy state QKD has a lower key rate when compared to other QKD systems using the same technique, while also being more vulnerable to this type of attack.

There has been a significant increase in the use of pre-trained language models for various natural language understanding tasks, particularly when it comes to performing well with minimal training data. The most effective strategy so far has been few-shot in-context learning, where the model is provided with a small number of examples along with a query and then generates a response based on that input. While it is widely accepted that pre-trained language models excel at this approach due to their ability to learn general linguistic patterns, there has been a prevailing hypothesis that models also acquire task-specific knowledge through this method. However, our review of recent studies challenges this hypothesis and instead highlights that the apparent knowledge transfer may actually result from the models filtering out irrelevancies in the context data. Moreover, we identify three critical factors influencing this phenomenon: model consistency, accurate generation of responses, and models with high perplexity still being able to perform well with fewer examples. As a final point, we offer practical recommendations to enhance model performance with fewer examples and better utilize the available context.

We've studied the-shock thickness effect on the linear growth rate of the thermal instability (TWI) in galaxy clusters. Utilizing 1D and 2D hydrodynamic codes, we modified the standard Fourier law for heat transfer to incorporate a non-equilibrium state, resulting in 'cooled' shock waves. Introducing an anisotropic conduction factor, $\lambda_T = f_{CR}\lambda_{Sp}$, where $\lambda_{Sp}$ represents the standard Spitzer conduction, we found that introducing an anisotropic conduction factor, $f_{CR}$, reduces the growth rate of cold features. For the 1D code, this effect is minimal, as it is also the case for the 2D code. Additionally, we examined how to differentiate between co- and counter-current directions of thermal instability. For thin shocks, the direction matters and non-equilibrium cooling can lead to enhanced or reduced, or even halted growth of thermal instability. However, for thicker shocks, the direction has little effect, as it is also the case for thick co-current shocks with $f_{CR}=0.01$.

A BSM physics review focuses on recent $C\!P$ violation observations in beauty baryons and charm systems that don't align with the Standard Model, examining theoretical models such as composite extra dimensions, heavy $Z'$ particles, supersymmetry, and neutral轻 lepton exchange.

We have developed fresh insights into the dynamics of strings during high-energy collisions by confirming the validity of the Katkov-Melikhov-Tudorov theorem in a broader context. Our findings indicate that previously proposed amplitudes for scattering in the context of the Open Superstring theory, particularly at large energy and momentum values, satisfy four key principles: the high-energy and momentum limits' equivalence, conformal symmetry, the Weyl scaling property, and the underlying theory's inherent features. Our work also lays the groundwork for further research into understanding the behavior of superstrings under influence from background fields and the application of modern theoretical methods to the analysis of high-energy scattering.

In order to address the rising demand for online training and inference, a decentralized approach is adopted, utilizing edge computing facilities. The publication introduces strategies to optimize these facilities' energy consumption. The developed optimizations incorporate innovative techniques such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, peer-to-peer communication, power management, and migration of computational tasks. The strategies's efficacy is evaluated through integration into a virtualized software-defined networking-based edge computing system named MicroEdge, enabling fine-grained resource allocation via light-weight containers. The optimizations are adaptively configured through the use of reinforcement learning to tailor them to traffic patterns and resource allocations. The efficacy of the optimizations is confirmed by performance testing using learning-based traffic emulation and quantitative analysis utilizing standard statistical methods.

This research introduces a novel method utilizing an auto-encoding variational normalizing flow to learn a compact latent space capable of generating various speech styles. By analyzing the speech segment cluster tree structure, we discover that transients and steady-states are distinctly grouped, with each node on the tree representing a specific phoneme and its corresponding speech style. An auto-encoder is then used to learn a normalizing flow in the potential space, and the transition from a transient to a steady-state is visualized and controlled in the learned potential space, while maintaining the same speech style. Additionally, the difference between transient and steady-state representations is examined and analyzed in the learned space.

This paper presents a novel, comprehensive method to increase the movement efficiency of multi-limbed robots through sensorless feedback. Utilizing multi-stage robot configuration planning in conjunction with real-time feedback, our optimization process significantly reduces the frequency of interactions between planning cycles and actual movement cycles. The initial stage involves a global optimization cycle generating a sequence of movements, while the subsequent stages execute these plans through local adjustments, ensuring swift execution of each movement cycle. Furthermore, our system incorporates mechanisms for handling unforeseen events during adjustments to maintain safety, such as stopping the robot or reducing its speed, which can be modified based on computational capacity without reducing the pace of optimizations. The optimization cycles take into account the interactions between the robot's limbs through soft constraints on cost functions that can be updated in real-time. Additionally, this framework has the capacity to adapt the optimizations in response to changes the robot's weight distribution during movements, thus preventing artifacts that could lead to suboptimal motions or incorrect forces. The effectiveness of our proposed system has been demonstrated through simulations of various complex movements in three-stage robots, including picking up objects and manipulating manipulanda, as well as through live experiments on robots with different numbers of stages and limbs.

In various contexts where non-trivial resources are inherent, a fundamental inquiry involves how to obtain states that are highly endowed with these resources. Focusing on situations with limited resources, we investigate the systematic distillation of states that are highly resource-rich by applying a single-use process, allowing for at most a minimal amount of error. We explore characterizing the boundaries between different outcomes and errors in distilling states that are highly resource-rich. We apply this approach to two specific quantum resource theories under specific constraints, revealing that the boundaries can be effectively represented using conventional tools from information theory in these scenarios. We apply our analysis to two particular quantum distillation scenarios to demonstrate its practical utility.

This research explores the dynamic behavior of a coffee cup when in motion. Unlike the traditional method of analyzing this scenario, which focuses on the fluid's response to a moving container walls, our approach treats the liquid as the primary system affected by the pivot-induced disturbances. By utilizing a coffee spill experiment, our study verifies both the theoretical predictions and previously reported outcomes, revealing that the experimentally observed phenomena align closely with the former findings. Additionally, our work highlights the limitations of existing theories in accurately predicting the coffee cup's response to external disturbances, emphasizing the need for further refinement of current models.

We are examining the accuracy of solutions achieved by distributed block coordinate descent methods in learning problems with strongly convex objectives and differentiable constraints. Analyzing a method that combines gradient tracking with stochastic gradient descent on decentralized systems with finite Q stages, non-negative constraint optimization via projected gradient descent, and evaluating convergence relative to the original problem without simplifying to an equivalent problem. We establish that the proposed method produces outputs within $\epsilon$ of the optimal solution within $\tilde{O}(\frac{n^2}{Q}\sqrt{L_\mathcal{G}}\frac{1}{\epsilon} n^2 \mu^{-2} + n^2\mu^{-1} + \mu n)^{Q}$ iterations, requiring only $\tilde{O}(\frac{n^2}{Q}\sqrt{L_\mathcal{G}}\epsilon^{-1} + n^2\epsilon^{-4})$ stages of size $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon})$ for reaching such outputs, where $n$ represents the number of decentralized nodes, $\mu$ and $L_\mathcal{G}$ denote the strong convexity constant and smoothness constant of the global objective, and we argue that $\tilde{O}(\frac{n^2}{Q}\sqrt{L_\mathcal{G}}\epsilon^{-1} + n^2\epsilon^{-4})$ depends on standard complexity measures, implying dependence on $n$ is at

Our investigation into the pre-equilibrium phase of nucleus-nucleus collisions utilizes the Kirkwood nonequilibrium statistical operator to explore how chaotic variables impact particle creation before a collision reaches equilibrium. By applying this approach, we successfully model various charged particle yields and find that the degree of nonequilibrium significantly influences final particle production. Furthermore, using this method and incorporating particle creation and partition methods, we examine the evolution of a nonequilibrium system in nucleus-lead collisions and model the creation of the particle $\rm U\^+$.

A theoretical model incorporating early mass accretion and mass loss phases in forming stars is presented, and the effects of core mass ratio and accretion efficiency on stellar formation are examined within low-mass star forming clouds. Our model indicates that mass ejection is a necessary component in the early stages of star formation as the protostar has not yet become radiatively stable. Following mass ejection, mass accretion takes place and the massive envelopes around the core collapse within the timescale that scales with core mass. The high mass accretion rate to the central protostar can be as high as the solar mass per year, and the protostar-forming region's radius decreases rapidly as the massive envelopes around the core collapse. The high mass accretion rate is likely the reason why young star polynomials like the age-mass relation exhibit significant scatter in mass. The high mass accretion rate in the early stages of star formation can be the reason for the presence of massive stars in the universe.

In safety-critical systems, maintaining stability is essential and requires careful control of variables that influence system behavior. Deviations in these variables can lead to unsafe conditions until corrective measures restore equilibrium. A key decision support concept for improving safety is hazard notification, which prompts compensation for the effects of destabilizing variables. However, existing hazard notification methods have a limitation in accurately representing the concept of threshold, as they rely on fixed boundary conditions that do not reflect the complex dynamics of hazardous variables. To overcome this challenge, a new mathematical model for hazard notification threshold has been developed, which uses a dynamic threshold function that evolves over time, allowing for more accurate detection of hazardous conditions. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through a fire safety example, which highlights its potential to enhance safety in practical applications.

An uncontrolled object may experience significant variations in orbital eccentricity and inclination due to the interaction of Solar Radiation Pressure and its orbital resonances. To identify the risks of such interactions, an efficient method is needed to quickly determine whether a particular object is in or close to a resonance of type I. Building on a fast-converging set of rules initially designed for resonances of type II, this paper introduces a comparable approach for identifying resonances of type I, also known as cot-type resonances. It incorporates two key adjustments: one accounting for the combined effect of SRP and drag force, and the other ensures that the rules converge within a narrow range of n-a_j values. To validate its effectiveness, this approach is compared with the traditional, step-by-step technique, resulting in a substantial reduction in identification time - around 500 times faster in the case of objects at risk of resonance and as much as 20 times faster for non-resonant objects.

We present a modified velocity operator for the widely-used tight-binding model that better describes an electron's response to an external electric field. Our findings indicate that by correcting the velocity operator in tight-binding models, we can significantly enhance their accuracy in calculating electromagnetic properties, an issue that has largely been overlooked until now.

The traditional EM algorithm, widely used for tracking objects with 2D data, often struggles with substantial translation and outliers due to its local convergence and sensitivity to initialization. We overcome these limitations by developing a graph-theoretic approach that integrates multiple optimization techniques. Our novel cost function uses vertex and edge observations to estimate an object's position, orientation, and size, all while maintaining consistency. By combining this method with RANSAC and robust optimization, we can effectively handle outliers of any size and ensure consistent results. Additionally, we employ iterative refinement in a global optimizer to further reduce estimation errors. Our algorithm's capability to converge globally is also analyzed. Our algorithm, introduced as RANSAR, has been evaluated in multiple scenarios and has been implemented in a real-world object-tracking application, which has been validated through extensive numerical analysis and a long-term numerical experiment, as well as through video footage, which has been made available online.

We examine the causal inference of a two-dimensional random variable $Z$ $following a Cauchy distribution, characterized by parameters $\theta = (\alpha, \beta)$ representing center and scale. Given independent observations of $Z$, our objectives are to estimate $\alpha$, $\beta$, or both, accompanied by the construction of confidence regions. Employing maximum likelihood estimation and empirical Bayes methods, our analysis reveals that the confidence regions for the estimated parameters take the shape of ellipses, aligning with prior results on causal Z-estimators. Furthermore, the study extends to determining confidence intervals or regions when $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is the parameter of interest, revealing corresponding rectangular shapes or sectors in the complex plane, respectively.

In clinical trial settings with patients exhibiting periodic variations, a statistical technique known as borrowing information between commensurate subgroups offers a valuable analytical approach. When treatment periods are harmonious with the patient measurement schedules, this borrowing can be carried out using closed-form equations. This paper presents a Monte Carlo simulation assessing the impact of commensurate methods on trial efficiency when accounting for time-shifts or 'phase shifts' in patient data. We compare three analytical approaches: one that ignores phase shifts, one that considers them using commensurate weighting, and one that uses a linear mixed model for analysis. Our findings indicate that weighting commensurately allows treatment groups to utilize additional data from patient readings, while the LMM model may assign greater importance to commensurate readings as it is specified to account for phase effects. Both of these methods require a smaller sample size than the approach that ignores phase shifts, while also providing accurate type-I error rates and statistical power. The results indicate that enrolling roughly 20% more patients can yield significant gains in power when commensurate information is utilized.

This study examines how spatial variations in dynamics influence motion control performance. Most modern motion control systems employ PID controllers due to their straightforward design, yet these controllers' effectiveness can be significantly diminished by dynamic inconsistencies across the moving platform. Unlike prior research focusing on parameter robustness, this work investigates the impact of geometric control design on tracking efficiency. Utilizing numerical simulation and experimental validation, this investigation evaluates the roles of PID control, nominal parameters, and spatial dynamics variations on tracking accuracy.

We develop a deep learning approach for object classification that leverages the
transformed latent space features from our previously developed Object Registration
Network (ORN). By incorporating the power of object registration into classification,
we enhance recognition performance, especially when objects appear in unexpected
orientations. To achieve this, we train ORN in an unsupervised manner using only
object identity labels and exploit its implicitly learned, object-aligned feature
space to perform classification. This groundbreaking approach has the potential to be
applied not just to class identification but also to other tasks such as similarities
assessment, virtual assembly, and object manipulation. Notably, ORN's capability to
align objects without corresponding point matches allows us to use it to match objects
that lack point correspondences. Experimental results showcase the superiority of our
object-aligned feature space in various scenarios, outperforming conventional object
classification methods.

Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a class of groups closed under taking subgroups and quotients.
The $\mathcal{N}$-nilpotency degree of a group $G$ is defined as the smallest positive integer $c$ such that the largest subgroup of $G$ belonging to $\mathcal{N}$ has nilpotency degree (as defined by Hall) no greater than $c$.
This paper examines $\mathcal{N}$-nilpotency degrees for specific group classes, focusing on p-groups and p-groups with prime power exponent.
Key relationships between key functions of certain group classes are established, and several $\mathcal{N}$-nilpotency degree formulas or bounds are derived for groups with prime power exponent.

A comprehensive two-year measurement of the top quark mass $m_t$ is proposed as a key objective for a small e+e- collider or a muon collider demonstrator. Utilizing advanced techniques such as inclusive methods and techniques of likelihood and profiling, it is demonstrated that these machines can achieve precise determination of $m_t$ without requiring precise formation of resonant states. Furthermore, it is shown that measuring the differential cross section $d\sigma/dm_{tt}$ can also yield a precise value for $m_t$ and the strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$. We have developed a specialized Monte Carlo event generator called TOPDEMONT to simulate the differential cross section $d\sigma/dm_{tt}$, and our generator is now publicly available.

Determining reaction coordinates utilizing data from ultrafast experiments often becomes difficult when exposed to noise. By analyzing spectra measured at various time points, a new method is proposed that can efficiently invert experimental data. Notably, this approach is insensitive to noise and does not necessitate data smoothing, a common practice that can sometimes distort results. To validate its efficacy, the algorithm is applied to simulated spectra of two-model systems and real spectra of a conformational switch.

Utilizing QCD sum rules, we analyze the vertex functions involving the $\rho$, $\rho^*$, and $D_s^*$ mesons in order to evaluate their distribution amplitudes. The results indicate that the distribution amplitudes of the $\rho$ and $\rho^*$ mesons are relatively uniform, implying an equal momentum distribution among their constituent quarks due to isovector symmetry. Conversely, the distribution amplitude of the $D_s^*$ meson exhibits asymmetry, with the heavy charm quark carrying the majority of its momentum. Furthermore, this study reveals that the mass of light quarks significantly influences the nonperturbative behavior of these mesons, leading to a substantial difference in their coupling factors - around three times larger for the $\rho$ compared to the $D_s^*$.

We investigate the growth estimates of Fourier transforms associated with functions and distributions within the Gelfand-Shilov spaces $\mathcal{B}^{\rho,\varphi,s}$. Specifically, the function $\varphi$ determines the log-convex weight applied to both the functions and their Fourier transforms. Our research yields new results for Fourier transforms associated with functions and distributions in $\mathcal{B}^{\rho,s,\varphi}$ by incorporating the theory from the paper "Non-newborn spaces and Fourier transforms" [25].

This paper introduces an innovative instance segmentation approach, called Co-occurring Feature Learning by Adversarial Disentangled Representation, that learns a shared compressed representation from multiple images, which uniquely identifies each instance when combined with its corresponding decoded features. By using deep generative models to represent multiple images, our method naturally handles various challenges such as novel object poses, occlusions, and different object sizes. To effectively separate image instances through deep latent coding, our framework employs a novel support vector quantization loss. Furthermore, the proposed CySGAN approach has superior segmentation performance, outperforming existing methods on challenging object categories with rich object properties. The proposed method also significantly reduces the dimension of existing object segmentation networks by forcing multiple images to share a single instance of deep latent coding, which can be used for various instance instance segmentation tasks. The approach is demonstrated to be effective on natural language and object segmentation tasks, and the corresponding code is available at https://github.com/hasanh07/CoarseToFineSGAN.

Effective action prediction requires modeling local interdependencies among body parts, regardless of their spatial arrangement. Traditional methods employing Recurrent Neural Networks focus on temporal patterns, but overlook the significance of radial patterns among body parts. This paper presents a novel architecture, EMAN2, that integrates temporal modeling with radial modeling for accurate and early action prediction. By using Edman's template for radial pattern extraction and Recurrent Neural Networks, EMAN2 outperforms state-of-the-art models on CHALLENGE and UMdB action benchmarks, achieving improvements of around 4% in prediction accuracy at the same frame.

Observations of the active K-type star AD Leo in the optical and UV bands were conducted using the UVIT instrument on board the AstroSat satellite, during a stellar flare in the far-UV range were key findings of this study. The data revealed that the star's far-UV emission peaks approximately 400-500 seconds after the optical peak, suggesting a higher time delay between the production of optical and UV photons. The UV bands emission peaking at a lower value, suggests a lower albedo for these wavelengths. The study revealed that the star's hydrogen lines in the optical and far-UV range were broadened by not more than 30 km s-1 and 60 km s-1 respectively, suggesting a lower value compared to other similar stars. The study reveals a direct proportionality between the star's hydrogen line broadening and the UVI and UV2 bands flux at the time of the flare. The study reveals a power law fit with a slope of 1.22 ± 0.3 for the UVI + UV2 bands energy integrated during a flare and the width of the H-beta (0.3041 μm) absorption line. We specifically investigate abelian instantons that are G2-invariant, focusing on analyzing their behavior. This involves defining families of such instantons and examining their relative properties. Our investigation also highlights the infinality of these families and enables us to identify specific points within a G2-instanton's moduli space that exhibit minimal energy characteristics.

To determine the normality of operators, we initially establish the normality of the shift operator in the space $H^2(\mathbb{B}_n)$. Subsequently, we identify the constraints under which a composition operator and a weighted composition operator are $C$-normal in $H^2(\mathbb{B}_n)$. Finally, we extend this analysis to the space $A^2(\mathbb{B}_n)$.

This explanation delves into the basics of the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions, which can be understood through the lens of a $p$-group. To accomplish this, we first establish connections between the $p$-regular classes of a $p$-group and specific partitions, namely the $p$-adic French valuation table. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the $p$-mapping $f$ transforms the set of all $p$-partitions, denoted as $\mathcal{P}_p(n)$, onto the set of its $p$-cores, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_p(n)$. Furthermore, within $\mathcal{C}_p(n)$, the $p$-cores of rank $k$, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_p^k(n)$, contain the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions, denoted as $f(g_n)$.

Machine learning models for point clouds are increasingly being used, but their vulnerability to geometric attacks poses a threat to their reliability, especially when relying on fixed data representations. The accuracy of such models can be significantly compromised by slight distortions in the input data, leading to substantial degradation in their performance. This research introduces the Trusted Geometry Platform, a robust method for enhancing the security of point cloud models against geometric manipulations. The platform consists of two key components: the Perfect Point Generation module, which produces idealized, regularized input representations to mitigate the impact of geometric attacks; and the Perturbed Training module, that trains the model with various idealized versions of the input data to increase its resilience. The Kullback-Leibler divergence guides TPC in exploring a manageable range of idealized input variations, thus reducing the computational costs associated with security-enhanced model training. The experimental results show that TPC can boost the point cloud model's certified accuracy against geometric manipulations by as much as 15%.

We assess small-scale Free-Mode Change Wave (FMCW) radar systems, which operate in a shared band at the physical layer, and focus on the packet structure used to reduce interference. To evaluate performance, we develop mathematical models for key metrics, including interference probability, packet drop rate, system throughput, and delay, based on both single and multiple chirps per packet scenarios. We validate our findings using simulations, highlighting how varying the number of chirps per packet impacts overall system performance and trade-offs. Additionally, we discuss design considerations to optimize the packet structure for effective conflict avoidance in FMCW radar networks.

Our study explores the theory and experiments of Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry involving one and two photons absorbed in non-linear materials. The visibility of the Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram is directly related to the detection of entangled two-photon absorption, which is a demonstration of the quantum nature of the process. The interplay between visibility and visibility oscillations offers a powerful tool for examining the entangled two-photon absorption process, allowing for the distinction between viable theories and a clear comprehension of its quantum nature.

We develop a highly flexible T-equivariant elliptic cohomology spectrum, denoted as $\EE_{\Ell, T}$, which can be seen as an equivalent of oriented elliptic cohomology, but specifically for the torus T. As a result, we establish a related, more specialized cohomology theory, specifically designed for torus actions within abelian varieties, by using $\EE_{\Ell, T}$ to establish a cohomology theory, denoted as $\EE_{X/T, T}$. This new theory features a simplified relationship with ordinary cohomology in a specific equivariant setting. Furthermore, we define a generalized equivariant elliptic cohomology theory for general algebraic groups by utilizing the most general elliptic scheme possible and also establish a connection between it and a specialized group-cohomology, similar to the non-equivariant scenario.

This work addresses the task of knowledge graph embedding, where subgraphs from temporal knowledge graphs are utilized to predict missing entities. A key challenge in this problem lies in accurately representing entities within temporal contexts. We introduce a novel encoding scheme that captures cyclic patterns and adapt it to the Knowledge Graph Embedding task. This scheme is complemented by a context-aware time-encoding scheme to account for time intervals in temporal knowledge graphs. Our method is implemented using a neural network and evaluated on several benchmark datasets, including CE-MSR, MN, and 24-ML, and demonstrates superior performance in predicting unknown entities in temporal knowledge graphs.

We've developed a straightforward technique to model ground sound generated by object collisions with varying surfaces like concrete, cobblestone, and grass. In our testing, we discovered that the sound generated by objects impacting softer materials or surfaces with soft coverings is generally unheard of, whereas collisions with concrete produce sound that can be heard about 1 meter away. We also modelled the sound propagation distance using a concrete impact as a reference for other surface types. In this model, colliding with cobblestone produces approximately 75% of the concrete impact's audible volume at 1 meter, cobblestone's lost volume plus the distance sound travels to hear that specific volume at cobblestone's surface (roughly 4 meters) is equivalent to hearing that volume on concrete at 1 meter. In contrast, hearing the sound generated by objects impacting with grass is usually inaudible, with an exception being when low-pitched sounds are produced, like when people jump on the grass.

Our investigation delves into the prevalence of idealized scenarios that facilitate experimental verification of Bell nonlocality's extreme qualities, a topic of significant importance for emerging quantum information technologies. Subsequent to examining numerous binary scenarios, we shift our focus to specific real-world applications of quantum information, revealing that even when considering realistic conditions, these scenarios exhibit remarkable tolerance to imperfections. This discovery holds substantial implications for the future of Bell nonlocality's applications and research within the quantum information technology domain.

Systems exhibiting highly degenerate flat bands are uncommon in nature, yet they exist in certain crystalline materials, topological tessellated arrays, and numerical models of random systems. Our investigation into the topology of random systems revealed that in a su(2) symmetric model, coupling variability preserves degeneracy, whereas coupling randomness in a generic su(2) broken symmetric model reduces degeneracy. Furthermore, we explored how system degeneracy impacts localization, utilizing a version of the Moore-Penrose inverse, developed for systems with incomplete coupling, to calculate inverse body diagonals in both su(2) symmetric and broken su(2) models. Our findings indicate that in su(2) symmetric models, coupling randomness doesn't affect the localization phase, whereas in broken su(2) models, sufficient randomness can induce a delocalization phase, with delocalized states being parabolic in nature due to the system's residual degeneracy.

Research on two-dimensional (2D) materials has gained momentum due to its potential in driving future nanotechnology advancements. The study of electron-phonon interaction in various 2D materials has produced significant results, revealing their unique optical, electrical, and thermal characteristics. With the emergence of advanced synthesis techniques, the creation of novel compounds such as hydrogen boride monolayers (BMNs) is now feasible. BMNs have the ability to combine electron-phonon coupling with hydrogen-rich properties. Our analysis using the density functional perturbation theory indicates that monolayers consist of a hexagonal honeycomb structure with a lattice constant of 3.215~\AA{}. BMNs exhibit a high thermal stability, with a phonon frequency of 64.7 cm^-1. Notably, they display unusual electrical and optical properties, exhibiting an indirect band gap of 2.18 eV. BMNs display large anisotropy in their optical response due to their unique electronic properties. Hydrogen's presence significantly affects the band structure and enhances electron-phonon interaction, yielding an electron-phonon coupling constant of 2.005. Furthermore, BMNs display quantum confinement properties, exhibiting metallic behavior in thick stacks and maintaining their optical anisotropy up to 10 nm thickness. Consequently, BMNs hold promise for applications in optoelectronics and thermoelectrics.

This note examines the flattened portions of specific sequences, such as those representing the number of permutations with $k$ runs and $k$ exponents of $-1$ in their descent runs. We employ generating functions to establish a set of recursive relationships for these sequences, where $f_{n, k}$ is used to describe the count of these permutations.

We examine dynamical systems arising from linear actions of finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups on the space of characters in the space of real Lie algebras for these groups. Our main contribution lies in contrasting the behavior of these group actions on this space with similar actions found in toroidal dynamics, specifically highlighting the distinct recurrence properties they exhibit. As a consequence, we identify a category of virtuously nilpotent groups that exhibit a divergence property akin to that seen in hyperbolic groups.

Evaluating the functional safety of automotive driving systems using formal verification techniques like model checking involves model creation which can be modeler-dependent and model complexity can lead to model checking limitations due to model size. It is crucial to enhance the comparability and reproducibility of the analysis and mitigate modeling ambiguities. This paper explores three methods to enhance model checking reliability and is compared through two case studies of automotive driving systems: a adaptive cruise control and a sophisticated routing algorithm models. These models were developed in two different models using formal modeling languages - state machines and process networks. Their comparison reveals the benefits of process networks in creating smaller models for model checking, resulting in a complete coverage of the verification requirements and consistent model checking results. Process networks provide a unique and clear model creation method for functional safety analysis, leading to functional safety reports with clear evidence of system safety.

This paper offers an in-depth examination of the application of the Koopman operator to resolve questions in nonlinear dynamics and provides a thorough comparison of existing methodologies in the literature.

In the early 18th century, significant debates surrounded infinite concepts, notably highlighted in critiques of Nicolas Berouille's book, which notably included criticism of Leibniz's views on infinity. These interpretations, which notably included those of Malebranche, initially distinguished between bounded and unbounded infinities in Leibniz's philosophy. However, by the late 18th century, such interpretations had become standard in understanding his philosophical stance. This article aims to clarify misconceptions about 18th-century interpretations of Leibniz's views on bounded and unbounded infinities by demonstrating the continuity between these concepts and those of limited and unlimited infinities. To achieve this, we will explore instances where Leibniz used the terms bounded/unbounded in analogy with limited/unlimited infinities. Our analysis is based primarily on his philosophical writings, which notably include the Opuscules et lettres, as well as his theological texts like the Elements of Natural Theology. By clarifying these distinctions, we will also demonstrate the continuity between the terms bounded/unbounded and limited/unlimited infinities when used to describe metaphysical entities, while noting discrepancies when applying the terms to mathematical objects. In the context of mathematical entities, which notably include geometrical and arithmetic objects, bounded/unbounded infinities are not opposed in the same way that limited/unlimited infinities are. This unique characteristic reflects the uniqueness of Leibniz's mathematical philosophy.

Gravitational lensing of the CMB is a valuable method for determining cosmological parameters and weak lensing of galaxies is an equally valuable tool for studying these parameters and dark energy, all at an even higher precision in the future. A major obstacle preventing us from achieving these goals today and being able to tackle these problems in the near future is the difficulty of separating the lensing signals from other signals within the observing bands for CMB and all observing for weak lensing of galaxies are contaminated by foregrounds such as galaxies, clusters and dust.
